impact: According to Section 26, an organisation may only transfer personal data outside Singapore if it has taken appropriate steps to ensure that: - it will comply with the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) obligations in respect of the transferred personal data while it remains in its possession or under its control; and - the recipient outside of Singapore is bound by legally enforceable obligations to provide a standard of protection to the personal data transferred that is comparable to that under the PDPA. In this regard, “legally enforceable obligations” would include obligations imposed on the recipient: (i) under law (e.g. the recipient’s relevant national data privacy legislation); (ii) under any contract: (a) requiring the recipient to provide a standard of protection to the personal data transferred that is at least comparable to the protection under the PDPA; and (b) specifying the countries and territories to which the personal data may be transferred under the contract; (iii) under binding corporate rules (see below); or (iv) any other legally binding instrument. laws: Personal Data Protection Act 2012
Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Act 2020
impact: The Personal Data Protection Act 2012 (PDPA) provides a baseline standard of protection for personal data in Singapore. It complements sector-specific legislative and regulatory frameworks such as the Banking Act and Insurance Act, Healthcare Services Act, Telecommunications Act, etc. The PDPA comprises various requirements governing the collection, use, disclosure and care of personal data in Singapore. Personal Data Protection Commission (PDPC) administers and enforces the PDPA. Moreover, the PDPA amendment in 2021 introduces a number of key reforms, including mandatory data breach notification requirements, amendments to the consent obligation, offences for egregious mishandling of personal data, prohibitions relating to the use of dictionary attacks and address-harvesting software, and the PDPC's power to accept voluntary undertakings as part of its enforcement regime.

laws: Cybersecurity Act 2018
impact: Cybersecurity Act 2018 establishes a legal framework for the oversight and maintenance of national cybersecurity in Singapore. The key objectives of the Cybersecurity Act are to: (i) strengthen the protection of Critical Information Infrastructure against cyber-attacks; (ii) authorize the government to prevent and respond to cybersecurity threats and incidents; (iii); establish a framework for sharing cybersecurity information, and (iv) establish a licensing framework for cybersecurity service providers. Amendments to the Act were made in May 2024 to update the Act so that it keeps pace with the developments in the cyber threat landscape, as well as our evolving technological operating context. The key amendments: (i) updated existing provisions relating to cybersecurity of Critical Information Infrastructure, and (ii) expanded CSA’s oversight to cover new classes of regulated entities.

laws: Privacy Act 1988
impact: The Privacy Act 1988 is the primary federal legislation that governs protection of personal information and applies horizontally. The Act includes thirteen Privacy Principles, which set out standards, rights and obligations for the handling, holding, use, accessing and correction of personal information (including sensitive information. The Privacy Act's amendment in 2018 introduced a mandatory notification scheme for entities in responding to data breaches. The Notifiable Data Breach Scheme (NDB scheme) introduced an obligation to notify individuals whose personal information is involved in a data breach that is likely to result in serious harm. The NDB scheme applies to all agencies and organisations with existing personal information security obligations under the Australian Privacy Act. The Privacy Act's amendment in 2023 increases the maximum penalties for serious or repeated privacy breaches and provides the Australian Information Commissioner with greater powers to resolve privacy breaches and quickly share information about data breaches.

laws: Privacy Impact Assessment 2020
impact: A Privacy Impact Assessment ('PIA') is contemplated by Australian privacy law but, apart from government agencies, is not mandated. In addition, the OAIC may, in writing, direct an agency to conduct a PIA, within a specified period if an agency proposes to engage in an activity or function involving the handling of personal information about individuals, and the OAIC considers that the activity or function might have a significant impact on the privacy of individual (Section 33D(1) of the Privacy Act).

laws: Personal Data Protection Act (Act 709) 2010

impact: The Personal Data Protection Act (Act 709) 2010 (PDPA) prohibits the transfer of personal data out of Malaysia unless such transfer is to a country, which has been specified and recorded in the Official Gazette by the Minister. Currently, no countries have been specified officially. Notwithstanding the prohibition on transfers of personal data out of the country, the PDPA sets out a number of exceptions to the prohibition, such as where the consent of the data subject has been obtained for such transfer and where the transfer is necessary for the performance of a contract between the parties. When in doubt as to whether the exemptions on data transfer apply, the prudent approach would be to obtain consent from the data subject in respect of such out of Malaysia transfer. In relation to outsourcing, a data user is not allowed to share data with third parties unless the consent of the individual has been obtained. The PDPA applies broadly across sectors to regulate the processing of personal data for commercial transactions. Any personal data processed in Malaysia must adhere to PDPA standards, including specific security and privacy principles. Section 6 requires that personal data should not be processed unless the data subject consents, or it is necessary for specific legal reasons. The Security Principle in Section 9 enforces practical steps to protect personal data from unauthorized or accidental access during processing, which aligns with local data storage requirements. Section 129 of the PDPA mentions restrictions on transferring personal data to places outside Malaysia unless the destination has data protection laws or the transfer meets specific conditions. The Personal Data Protection Code of Practice for the Banking and Financial Sector 2017 mandates that personal data be processed according to PDPA principles. Specific rules about data transfer abroad are mentioned in the document, limiting cross-border data transfers without compliance. Similar requirements for the Communications Sector are set out in the Code of Practice for Licensees Under the Communications and Multimedia Act 1998, especially for network and service providers. Both banking and communications sectors mention compliance with the Data Transfer Abroad clause, ensuring that any cross-border data transfer adheres to Malaysia’s data protection standards duscussed in other relevant subpillars.

impact: Malaysia currently does not have a strict data localization law that mandates all personal data to be stored exclusively within the country. This means that while data can be stored and processed abroad, certain safeguards must be in place to protect personal data. For certain sectors, like banking and finance, there are sector-specific guidelines (e.g., the Banking and Financial Sector Code of Practice) that impose more stringent conditions on data transfers and suggest that local processing is preferable to ensure compliance with security and privacy standards. These requirements do not constitute a blanket local storage mandate but make local storage a practical solution for ensuring compliance with security obligations, especially for sensitive data.

laws: Services Tax Act (Act 807) 2018
impact: Section 24 of the Service Tax Act 2018 (Act 807) sets out the obligations for recordkeeping by taxable persons. Every taxable person must keep complete, accurate, and up-to-date records of all transactions that affect or may affect their liability to service tax. This includes records of all taxable services provided or received (such as invoices, receipts, debit and credit notes), records of imported taxable services, and any other records as may be determined by the Director General. These records must be preserved for seven years from the most recent date to which they relate, must be kept in either the national language or English, and must be retained in Malaysia unless otherwise approved by the Director General under specific conditions. If records are maintained in an electronically readable format, they must be stored in a way that allows for ready access and conversion into writing. If records originally kept in manual form are later converted to electronic form, the original manual versions must also be preserved. Copies of records are admissible in legal proceedings to the same extent as the originals. This section also applies to any person, other than a taxable person, who acquires imported taxable services in the course of business. Failure to comply with any of these requirements is an offence and may result in a fine of up to RM50,000, imprisonment of up to three years, or both. However, these obligations do not apply to foreign registered persons. Note that this requirement was available under the repealed Goods and Services Tax Act 2014.

laws: Income Tax Act (Act 53) 1967
impact: Section 82 imposes a legal duty on all businesses to maintain proper records and, where applicable, issue receipts. Every business must keep accurate and sufficient records for at least seven years from the end of the relevant income year to allow tax authorities to determine taxable income or losses. If gross takings exceed RM150,000 from goods or RM100,000 from services, the business must issue serially numbered printed receipts for each transaction and keep duplicates. Businesses that file late returns must also keep records for seven years from the filing date. If a sales recording machine is used, the receipt requirement may be waived, but only if the machine records all transactions accurately. The Director General may set or waive requirements for recordkeeping and receipts and may also request audited financial statements under the Companies Act 2016 if existing records are inadequate. Entries must be made within 60 days of each transaction. Records kept electronically must be readable, accessible, and convertible to written form; if manual records are later digitized, the originals must be preserved. Moreover, All records that relate to any business in Malaysia shall be kept and retained in Malaysia. This includes records of (a) books of account recording receipts and payments or income and expenditure; (b) invoices, vouchers, receipts and such other documents as in the opinion of the Director General are necessary to verify the entries in any books of account; and (c) any other records as may be specified by the Director General under subsection (3).

impact: The Personal Data Protection Act (Act 709) 2010 (PDPA) does not permit a data user to transfer any personal data out of Malaysia. However, the Act offers a set of exceptions, permitting the transfer of data abroad under certain conditions. Section 129 (Cross-border data transfers) prescribes that personal data shall be transferred to any location outside Malaysia if: - the data subject has given his explicit consent to the transfer; - the transfer is necessary for the performance of a contract between the data subject and the data user; - the transfer is necessary for the conclusion or performance of a contract between the data user and a third party that is either entered into at the request of the data subject or in his interest; - the transfer is in the exercise of or to defend a legal right; - the transfer mitigates adverse actions against the data subjects; - reasonable precautions and all due diligence to ensure compliance to conditions of the Act were taken; or - the transfer was necessary for the protection the data subject’s vital interests or for the public interest as determined by the Minister. Additionally, Section 6 – General Principle: Personal data shall not be processed unless the data subject consents to the processing, except in specific situations like fulfilling contractual obligations or complying with legal requirements. Section 9 – Security Principle: Data users must take practical steps to ensure personal data is protected against loss, misuse, modification, unauthorized access, or disclosure. This includes securing local processing and storage systems. The Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Bill 2024 (Act A1727) amendments to the PDPA introduce stricter controls on cross-border data transfers, requiring organizations to assess the recipient country’s data protection framework to ensure that adequate protections are in place before transferring data. This could further encourage local data storage as an easier compliance path. - In the Retention Principle (Section 3.1.5), Personal data should not be kept longer than necessary for the purpose it was collected. - In the Transfer of Personal Data Abroad, Section 4.11 prohibits the transfer of personal data abroad unless the recipient country ensures adequate protection under similar data protection laws or explicit consent from the data subject is obtained. - In the Conditions for Transfer in Schedule 1, Section 1.1(38): Any cross-border transfer must ensure compliance with the PDPA’s principles, particularly related to the security of data, and must have written agreements with third-party data processors abroad.

laws: Personal Data Protection Act (Act 709) 2010
Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Bill (Act A1727) 2024
impact: Malaysia has a comprehensive data protection framework established through the Personal Data Protection Act (Act 709) 2010, which applies to the processing of personal data in commercial transactions. The PDPA regulates how personal data can be collected, used, and disclosed, and it imposes obligations on data users (companies and organizations) to protect the personal data of individuals. Moreover, the Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Bill 2024 (Act A1727) amendments to the PDPA further enhance this framework by introducing mandatory data breach notifications, extending data processor obligations, and increasing penalties for non-compliance, aligning Malaysia’s privacy regulations more closely with international standards like the EU’s GDPR. Specifically, data Breach Notification (Section 12b) requires data controllers (including those in banking and communications sectors) to notify the Personal Data Protection Commissioner and affected data subjects in the event of a data breach, especially if the breach poses significant harm. Moreover, penalties (Amendment of Section 5) prescribes that the penalties for non-compliance with the Security Principle or data breach requirements have been increased to 1 million ringgit or imprisonment of up to three years, or both. In addition to the PDPA, sector-specific codes of practice also exist for industries like banking, finance, and communications, but these operate within the comprehensive legal framework provided by the PDPA.

laws: Computer Crimes Act (Act 563) 1997
Cyber Security Act (Act 854) 2024
impact: Malaysia previous cybersecurity law was based on Computer Crimes Act (Act 563) 1997, it criminalizes various cybercrimes, such as unauthorized access to computers, modification of computer content, and other malicious cyber activities. However, it mainly addresses cyber offenses rather than a broader cybersecurity framework. The Cyber Security Act 2024 now provides a comprehensive framework to address national cybersecurity threats and regulate service providers. The new Cyber Security Act (Act 854) 2024 enhances Malaysia’s national cybersecurity efforts by: 1. Establishing a National Cyber Security Committee, responsible for overseeing cybersecurity policies and national coordination (Part III - Duties and Powers of Chief Executive). 2. Defining roles for critical information infrastructure entities and mandating them to comply with cybersecurity risk assessments, audits, and notifications of cybersecurity incidents. Sections 15-24 cover the responsibilities and duties of entities designated as national critical information infrastructure. 3. Regulating cybersecurity service providers through a licensing regime to ensure that those offering services like managed security operation center monitoring and penetration testing adhere to national standards. Sections 27-34 focus on the licensing of cybersecurity service providers. 4. Strengthening enforcement through powers of investigation, search, and seizure, allowing the government to respond effectively to cybersecurity threats (Sections 36-52), thus, enabling the enforcement of cybersecurity regulations and the management of cyber incidents. This new law positions Malaysia to better handle cyber risks and threats to its critical infrastructures.

laws: Personal Data Protection Act (Act 709) 2010
Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Bill (Act A1727) 2024
Personal Data Protection Standard 2015
impact: The data retention requirements for personal data are generally governed by the Personal Data Protection Act (Act 709) 2010 (PDPA). The PDPA 2010 enforces the Retention Principle, which requires data to be kept only as long as necessary for the purpose for which it was collected. However, this principle allows individual sectors to set their own retention periods based on operational needs or other regulatory obligations. In addition to the retention principle under the PDPA, the 2015 Standards outline the main standards for data retention which apply to personal data which is processed either electronically or non-electronically. A brief overview of the measures prescribed by the 2015 Standards are as follows: 1) to ensure that all legislation relating to the processing and storing of personal data is complied with before disposing of personal data; 2) not retaining personal data for longer than is required unless there are other legislative requirements that require personal data to be kept for a longer period; 3) to prepare and maintain records on the disposal of personal data and to submit these records when directed by the Commissioner; 4) to dispose of any personal data collection forms used for commercial transactions within 14 days, unless the form has legislative value in connection with the commercial transaction; 5) to review and dispose of all personal data that is no longer needed in the database; 6) to have a personal data disposal schedule for a period of 24 months for any inactive personal data; and to obtain written consent from the higher management of the data user's organization if using removable media devices for the purposes of personal data storage.

laws: Personal Data Protection Act (Act 709) 2010

impact: The Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Bill 2024 (Act A1727) amendments to the Personal Data Protection Act (Act 709) 2010 (PDPA) introduced new requirements, including the appointment of Data Protection Officers (DPOs) and the implementation of Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs), marking significant changes compared to the original PDPA 2010. Section 12a (1) of the 2024 PDPA amendment mandates that a data controller must appoint one or more Data Protection Officers (DPOs). The DPO is accountable for ensuring compliance with the PDPA, which applies horizontally across all sectors. This is a significant change from the 2010 version, where no explicit requirement for a DPO was mandated. The 2024 amendments also introduced a requirement for DPIAs in specific cases where data processing activities pose a high risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals. This is especially relevant for large-scale processing of sensitive personal data or new technologies. Similar to the DPO requirement, the DPIA requirement applies horizontally across all sectors when high-risk processing is involved. Another significant change from the 2010 PDPA, as organizations are now required to assess and mitigate risks through formal DPIA procedures.

Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Bill (Act A1727) 2024
impact: From the Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Bill 2024 (Act A1727) amendments, there is no explicit provision that allows the government to access personal data without a court order. The Personal Data Protection Act (Act 709) 2010 PDPA Section 45(2)(a)(i) exempts personal data from the consent requirement if it is processed for the prevention or detection of crime, or for the purposes of investigations. And Section 121 grants authorized officers the power to request the production of documents or data (including computerized data) to ensure compliance with the PDPA. An authorized officer shall have the powers of a police officer of whatever rank as provided for under the Criminal Procedure Code (Act 593) in relation to investigation, and such powers shall be in addition to and not in derogation of, the powers provided for under this Act (Section 112 Power of investigation). A Magistrate may issue a warrant for an officer to search premises and seize evidence related to an offense, with or without assistance and by force if needed (Section 113 Search and seizure with warrant). However, where delay could harm the investigation, an officer may search without a warrant using the same powers (Section 114 Search and seizure without warrant). These specific sectoral guidelines indicate that while court orders are generally required for accessing personal data, exceptions exist, particularly for criminal investigations and regulatory functions, where data can be accessed without consent or court intervention.

laws: Personal Data Protection Code of Practice for Licensees Under the Communications and Multimedia (Act 1998) of 2017
impact: As part of the broader legal and regulatory framework, law enforcement agencies and investigative authorities can request access to personal data under certain circumstances, as outlined in related sector-specific guidelines and laws such as the Communications and Multimedia Act 1998 (Section 7.4) applies when personal data is processed for the apprehension or prosecution of offenders, or when required for the assessment or collection of any tax or duty.

laws: Personal Data Protection Code of Practice For Banking Sector And Financial Institutions 2017
impact: The Banking and Financial Sector guidelines (Section 3.7.4) includes provisions for processing data for tax assessment or legal obligations, allowing such access without prior notice to the individual.

laws: Cyber Security Act (Act 854) 2024
impact: Section 46 of the Cyber Security Act (Act 854) 2024 concerning access to computerized data allows an authorized officer conducting a search under this Act to be given access to computerized data stored in computers or otherwise.The authorized officer means any policy officer of whatever rank or any public officer authorized by the Minister in writing (Section 4). An authorized officer shall have the powers of a police officer of whatever rank as provided for under the Criminal Procedure Code (Act 593) in relation to investigation, and such powers shall be in addition to and not in derogation of, the powers provided for under this Act (Section 38 Power of investigation). A Magistrate may issue a warrant for an officer to search premises and seize evidence related to an offense, with or without assistance and by force if needed (Section 39 Search and seizure with warrant). However, where delay could harm the investigation, an officer may search without a warrant using the same powers (Section 40 Search and seizure without warrant).

laws: Security Offences (Special Measures) Act (Act 747) 2012
impact: Under Section 6(3) of the Security Offenses (Special Measures) Act (Act 747) 2012 (Power to intercept communication), a police officer with the rank of superintendent of police or above may intercept communications without the authorization of the public prosecutor in urgent and sudden cases where immediate action is required leaving no moment of deliberation. Specifically, “communication” means a communication received or transmitted by post or a telegraphic, telephonic or other communication received or transmitted by electricity, magnetism or other means; “communications service provider” means a person who provides services for the transmission or reception of communications (Section 6(7)).

laws: Criminal Procedure Code (Act 593) 2018
impact: The Criminal Procedure Code (Act 593) 2018 Section 116B (Access to computerized data) of the Criminal Procedure Code provides that a police officer conducting a search under the Code must be given access to computerised data whether stored in a computer or otherwise. For the purpose of this section, 'access' includes being provided with the necessary password, encryption code, decryption code, software, or hardware and any other means required to enable comprehension of the computerised data. It is not clear whether a court order is needed to access the information. Additionally, Section 116C (Interception of communication) provides that the public prosecutor has the authority to authorize police officer to intercept, detain and open postal articles. This also includes intercept messages or conversations transmitted by any communication, and install devices on premises for intercepting communications. The Court shall take cognizance of any authorization by the Public Prosecutor under this section.

laws: Interim Measures for the Administration of Online Ride-Hailing Services《网络预约出租汽车经营服务管理暂行办法》
impact: Article 27: Ride-hailing platform companies shall comply with relevant national regulations on network and information security. The personal information collected and business data generated shall be stored and used within mainland China, with a retention period of no less than two years. Unless otherwise stipulated by laws and regulations, the aforementioned information and data shall not be transferred abroad.

laws: Interim Measures for the Administration of the Business Activities of Online Lending Information Intermediaries《网络借贷信息中介机构业务活动管理暂行办法》
impact: Article 27 states that for online lending information intermediaries shall strengthen the management of information related to lenders and borrowers, and ensure the legality and security of the collection, processing, and use of such information. The storage, processing, and analysis of information on lenders and borrowers collected within China shall be conducted within the territory of China. Except as otherwise provided by laws and regulations, online lending information intermediaries shall not provide information of domestic lenders and borrowers to parties outside of China.

laws: Regulations on the Administration of Credit Reporting Industry《征信业管理条例》
impact: Article 24: The collation, storage, and processing of information collected by credit reporting agencies within the territory of China shall be conducted within China.

laws: Administrative Measures for Population Health Information (For Trial Implementation) 《人口健康信息的管理措施（试行）》
impact: Article 10: Responsible entities shall update and maintain population health information in a timely manner according to service and management needs, ensuring that the information remains current, continuous, and effective. Population health information shall not be stored on servers located abroad, nor shall it be hosted or leased on overseas servers.

laws: Map Management Regulations 《地图管理条例》
impact: Article 34: Internet map service providers shall store map data on servers located within the territory of the People's Republic of China and establish an internet map data security management system along with protective measures.

laws: Data Protection Measure for Industrial and Telecom Companies 《工业和信息化领域数据安全管理办法（试行）》
impact: According to Article 3 of the Measures, Industrial data refers to data generated and collected during research and development, design, production, manufacturing, business management, operation and maintenance, and platform operation across various industries and fields within the industrial sector. Telecommunications data refers to data generated and collected during telecommunications business operations. Radio data refers to data generated and collected during radio business activities, including radio frequency data, station parameters, and other radio wave parameters. Furthermore, Chapter 2 classifies data into "general", "important" and "core", and require firms to take different degrees of protection measures when collecting, processing, transferring, and disposing of data. In particular, Article 21 states that data processors in the industrial and information technology sector that collect and generate important data and core data within the territory of the People's Republic of China shall store such data domestically if required by laws and administrative regulations. If it is necessary to provide the data abroad, a data export security assessment shall be conducted in accordance with laws and regulations.

laws: Personal Information Protection Law of the People's Republic of China《中华人民共和国个人信息保护法》
Cybersecurity Law of the People's Republic of China《中华人民共和国网络安全法》
impact: Under the Personal Information Protection Law (PIPL): Article 36: Personal information processed by state agencies shall be stored within the territory of the People's Republic of China. If it is necessary to provide such information abroad, a security assessment shall be conducted. The security assessment may require support and assistance from relevant departments. Article 40: Operators of critical information infrastructure and personal information processors that handle personal information in quantities specified by the national cybersecurity authority shall store the personal information collected and generated within the territory of the People's Republic of China. If it is necessary to provide such information abroad, a security assessment organized by the national cybersecurity authority must be conducted. If laws, administrative regulations, or provisions of the national cybersecurity authority exempt such security assessments, those provisions shall prevail. Similarly, Article 37 of the Cybersecurity Law states exactly the same with Article 40 of the PIPL.

laws: Interim Measures for the Administration of Online Ride-Hailing Services《网络预约出租汽车经营服务管理暂行办法》
impact: Article 27 states that online ride-hailing platform companies must comply with national regulations on cybersecurity and information security. The personal information collected and business data generated shall be stored and used within mainland China, with a retention period of no less than two years. Unless otherwise stipulated by laws and regulations, such information and data shall not be transferred abroad.

laws: Interim Measures for the Administration of Online Ride-Hailing Services《网络预约出租汽车经营服务管理暂行办法》
impact: Article 5 states that applicants seeking to engage in online ride-hailing operations must possess both online and offline service capabilities, have their servers located in mainland China, and implement network security management systems and security protection measures in compliance with regulations.

laws: Map Management Regulations 《地图管理条例》
impact: Article 34: Internet map service providers shall store map data on servers located within the territory of the People's Republic of China and establish an internet map data security management system along with protective measures.

laws: Administrative Regulations for Online Publishing Services《网络出版服务管理规定》
impact: Article 7: Engaging in online publishing services requires approval from the publishing administrative authority in accordance with the law and obtaining an Online Publishing Service License. Article 8: Publishing entities such as book, audiovisual, electronic, newspaper, and periodical publishers engaging in online publishing services must meet the following conditions: 1. Possess a designated publishing platform for online publishing activities, such as a website domain or an intelligent terminal application; 2. Have a clearly defined scope of online publishing services; 3. Have the necessary technical equipment required for online publishing services, with relevant servers and storage devices located within the territory of the People's Republic of China.

laws: Personal Information Protection Law of the People's Republic of China《中华人民共和国个人信息保护法》
impact: Chapter 3 of the Law stipulates Rules for Cross-Border Provision of Personal Information. Specifically, Article 38 states that if a personal information processor needs to provide personal information outside the People's Republic of China due to business or other needs, it must meet one of the following conditions: 1. Passing a security assessment organized by the national cybersecurity authority in accordance with Article 40 of this law; 2. Undergoing personal information protection certification by a professional institution in accordance with the regulations of the national cybersecurity authority; 3. Entering into a contract with the overseas recipient based on the standard contract formulated by the national cybersecurity authority, stipulating the rights and obligations of both parties; 4. Meeting other conditions stipulated by laws, administrative regulations, or the national cybersecurity authority. If an international treaty or agreement concluded or participated in by the People's Republic of China provides conditions for the cross-border provision of personal information, such provisions may be followed. Furthermore, Article 39 states that when a personal information processor provides personal information outside the People's Republic of China, they shall inform the individual of the name or identity of the overseas recipient, their contact information, the purpose and method of processing, the types of personal information involved, and the means and procedures for the individual to exercise their rights under this law with the overseas recipient. The processor must also obtain the individual's separate consent.

laws: Provisions on Promoting and Regulating Cross-border Data Flow《促进和规范数据跨境流动规定》
impact: The Provisions clarify the applicable standards for data processors in cross-border data transfers, including security assessment, standard contract for outbound transfer of personal data, and personal information protection certification. Critical information infrastructure operators (CIIOs) shall undergo a security assessment when transferring personal information or important data outside China. Other entities also need to conduct a security assessment when transferring important data or a large volume of personal information, with specific thresholds set at personal information (without sensitive personal information) of more than 1 million individuals or sensitive personal information of more than 10,000 individuals accumulated from January 1 of the current year. Furthermore, the Provisions includes specific scenario exemptions: Article 2: Data processors shall identify and report important data in accordance with relevant regulations. If the relevant authorities or regions have not notified or publicly designated the data as important data, data processors are not required to declare it as important data for a data export security assessment. Article 3: Data generated from international activities (e.g., trade, transportation, academic cooperation, manufacturing, marketing) that does not include personal or important data is exempt from cross-border data security assessments and compliance requirements. Article 4: Personal information collected abroad and processed in China before being transferred overseas, as long as no domestic personal or important data is involved, is exempt from cross-border data security assessments and compliance requirements. Article 5: Certain cross-border personal information transfers are exempt from security assessments and compliance requirements, including (1) fulfilling contracts (e.g., cross-border shopping, visa processing), (2) managing international human resources, (3) handling emergencies, and (4) transferring personal data abroad under a 100,000-person threshold (excluding sensitive data). Personal information provided abroad must not include important data.

laws: Personal Financial Information Protection Technical Specification《个人金融信息保护技术规范》
impact: Article 7.1.3, part (d) of the Techinical Specification states that in the process of providing financial products or services within the territory of the People's Republic of China, personal financial information collected and generated shall be stored, processed, and analyzed within the country. If it is necessary to provide personal financial information to overseas institutions (including headquarters, parent companies, branches, subsidiaries, and other affiliated institutions essential for completing the business) due to business requirements, the specific requirements are as follows: - It must comply with national laws and regulations as well as relevant provisions of the competent industry authorities; - Explicit consent must be obtained from the subject of the personal financial information; - A security assessment for the cross-border transfer of personal financial information must be conducted in accordance with the measures and standards established by relevant national and industry authorities to ensure that the data security protection capabilities of overseas institutions meet the security requirements of relevant national and industry authorities as well as financial institutions; - Agreements must be signed with overseas institutions, and on-site inspections shall be conducted to clarify and supervise the overseas institutions in effectively fulfilling their obligations, such as maintaining the confidentiality of personal financial information, data deletion, and case investigation cooperation.

laws: Personal Information Protection Law of the People's Republic of China《中华人民共和国个人信息保护法》
impact: The Personal Information Protection Law (PIPL) is applicable to any organization and individual who processes personal information in China. For companies outside China, the PIPL is also applicable if they provide services or products to people in China or analyze and evaluate the activities of people in China. The PIPL sets out the conditions for transfer of personal information out of China, protection of sensitive personal information, classification and retention of personal information and other compliance requirements.

laws: Data Security Law of the People's Republic of China《中华人民共和国数据安全法》
impact: On June 10, 2021, the Data Security Law of the People’s Republic of China was officially passed during the 29th session of the Standing Committee of the 13th National People’s Congress. Aiming to further strengthen the current protection regime for the country’s fast-growing digital economy, the law stipulates how data is used, collected, developed, and protected in China. It emphasizes on top-down coordination of data security implementation among local governments and differentiated fines based on severity of violations.

laws: Management Standards for the Entry and Removal of Digital Educational Resources on the National Smart Education Platform 《国家智慧教育平台数字教育资源入库出库管理规范》
Notice on Further Advancing the Electronic Information Management of Physicians 《关于进一步推进医师电子化信息管理工作的通知》
Interim Measures for Data Security Management of Accounting Firms 《会计师事务所数据安全管理暂行办法》
Implementation Plan for Establishing a Carbon Footprint Management System 《关于建立碳足迹管理体系的实施方案》
impact: In addition to comprehensive legislation that applies horizontally across all sectors, China has also developed and implemented a wide range of sector-specific regulations related to data protection, offering detailed guidance tailored to different industries. For example, in just the first half of 2024 alone, the Chinese government issued over 20 national laws, industry regulations, and local policies concerning data security. A selection of these is listed below. Education sector: The General Office of the Ministry of Education Issued the “Management Standards for the Entry and Removal of Digital Educational Resources on the National Smart Education Platform”. According to the Standards, platform service providers must comply with relevant laws, regulations, and national standards, and adopt technical and other necessary measures to ensure the security of the platform and its resources, as well as retain network logs in accordance with the law. Healthcare sector: The National Health Commission, the National Administration of Traditional Chinese Medicine, and the National Disease Control and Prevention Administration jointly issued the "Notice on Further Advancing the Electronic Information Management of Physicians". The Notice calls on local authorities to implement a data security accountability system, strengthen data security monitoring and early warning mechanisms, regularly conduct security assessments and risk evaluations, and establish disaster recovery and data backup systems to ensure the security of information within electronic registration systems. Finance sector: The Ministry of Finance and the Cyberspace Administration of China jointly issued the "Interim Measures for Data Security Management of Accounting Firms". The Measures require accounting firms to classify and categorize data in accordance with relevant laws, regulations, and the data classification standards applicable to the industry of the audited entity. Firms must identify core data, important data, and general data, and comply with specific requirements regarding the storage, transmission, and logging of core and important data. Energy sector: The Ministry of Ecology and Environment, together with 14 other departments, jointly issued the "Implementation Plan for Establishing a Carbon Footprint Management System". The Plan calls for strengthening the protection of data security and intellectual property related to product carbon footprints. It emphasizes the implementation of data security laws and regulations, enhanced oversight of data circulation, and the creation of a secure and reliable environment for data exchange. The Plan also encourages digital technology enterprises to provide cloud-based security services to improve overall data security standards.

laws: Cybersecurity Law of the People's Republic of China《中华人民共和国网络安全法》
Measures for Cybersecurity Review《网络安全审查办法》
National Emergency Response Plan for Cybersecurity Incidents《国家网络安全事件应急预案》
impact: The Cybersecurity Law, which came into force on 1 June 2017, is the law covering various aspects of network security and has laid the foundation for a comprehensive cybersecurity regulatory regime in China. So far, a series of specific measures aimed at facilitating the implementation of the Cybersecurity Law have already been enacted, such as the Measures for Cybersecurity Review and the National Emergency Response Plan for Cybersecurity Incidents.

laws: Regulation on Network Data Security Management《网络数据安全管理条例》
impact: Article 12: When a network data processor provides or entrusts the processing of personal information and important data to another network data processor, it shall agree on the processing purposes, methods, scope, and security protection obligations through a contract or other means with the data recipient, and shall supervise the fulfillment of these obligations by the data recipient. Records of the processing activities involving the provision or entrustment of personal information and important data to another network data processor must be kept for at least 3 years.

laws: Regulation on Internet Information Services of the People's Republic of China 《互联网信息服务管理办法》
impact: The Regulation on Internet Information Services of the People's Republic of China requires that Internet Service Providers (ISPs) keep records of each service user’s time spent online, user account, IP address or domain name, phone number and other information for 60 days and provide that information to the authorized government authorities when required (Article 14.).

laws: Interim Measures for the Administration of Online Ride-Hailing Services《网络预约出租汽车经营服务管理暂行办法》
impact: Article 27 states that online ride-hailing platform companies must comply with national regulations on cybersecurity and information security. The personal information collected and business data generated shall be stored and used within mainland China, with a retention period of no less than two years. Unless otherwise stipulated by laws and regulations, such information and data shall not be transferred abroad.

laws: Measures on the Administration of Accounting Records《会计档案管理办法》
impact: According to Article 14 of the measures, there are minimum retention periods for various accounting vouchers, accounts, books, financial reports and other accounting documents, and the retation periods are either 10 years or 30 years. Furthermore, certain key accounting records are subject to permanent retention. These records include: - Annual financial accounting reports - List of handover accounting records - List of retained accounting records - Accounting records evaluation opinion

laws: E-commerce Law of the People's Republic of China《中华人民共和国电子商务法》
impact: Article 31 of the Law states that all e-commerce platform business shall record and retain the information on the commodities and services and transaction information released in the platform and ensure the integrity, confidentiality and availability of the information. The information on commodities, services, and transactions shall be retained for at least three years from the day of completion of the transaction, unless otherwise provided by any law or administrative regulation.

laws: Personal Information Protection Law of the People's Republic of China《中华人民共和国个人信息保护法》
Guidance for Personal Information Security Impact Assessment (GB/T 39335–2020)《信息安全技术 个人信息安全影响评估指南》
impact: Article 52 of The Personal Data Protection Law states that: Where the quantity of personal information processed by a processor reaches that specified by the state cyberspace administration, the processor shall designate a person in charge of personal information protection to be responsible for supervising the processing of personal information and the adopted protection measures. A personal information processor shall make public the contact information of the person in charge of personal information protection and submit the name and contact information of the person in charge of personal information protection to the department performing duties of personal information protection. Furthermore, according to Article 55, a personal information processor shall conduct personal information protection impact assessment of the following circumstances in advance and keep a record of the processing: (I) processing sensitive personal information; (II) making use of personal information to make automatic decisions; (III) entrusting others to process personal information, providing other personal information processors with personal information, and disclosing personal information; (IV) providing personal information to overseas parties; and (V) other personal information processing activities that have a significant impact on individuals’ rights and interests. Guidance for Personal Information Security Impact Assessment (GB/T 39335 – 2020) ('the Security Impact Assessment Guidance') further provides detailed rules for personal information handlers on how to conduct protection impact assessment for high-risk data processing activities, e.g. processing sensitive personal information, providing personal information to another data handler, and cross-border transfer of personal information.

laws: Amendment to the Information Security Technology – Personal Information Security Specification (GB/T 35273-2020) 《信息安全技术-个人信息安全规范》（GB/T 35273-2020）修正案
impact: The 2020 Specification provides that personal information controllers shall appoint a person and a department responsible for personal information (PI) protection. Article 11.1 further stipulates that the person responsible for PI protection must be someone who has relevant management experience and personal information protection expertise and shall participate in important decisions on personal information processing activities and report directly to the principal of the organization. Article 11.1 further states that organizations meeting any of the following conditions should establish a dedicated personal information protection officer and a personal information protection work mechanism, responsible for personal information security work: 1. The primary business involves handling personal information, and the organization has more than 200 employees engaged in this business; 2. Processes personal information of over 1 million individuals, or is expected to process the personal information of over 1 million individuals within 12 months; 3. Processes the sensitive personal information of more than 100,000 individuals.

laws: Cybersecurity Law of the People's Republic of China《中华人民共和国网络安全法》
impact: Article 21 of the Cybersecurity Law requires network operators to appoint persons in charge of cybersecurity. Critical information infrastructure operators (CIIO) are also required to set up specialized security management bodies and persons responsible for security management. Further, CIIO's must conduct security background checks on those responsible persons and personnel in critical positions.

laws: Counter-Espionage Law of the People's Republic of China《中华人民共和国反间谍法》
impact: Article 25 and 26 of the Counterespionage Law provides for state security organ personnel to gain entry to restricted regions, venues or units and to inspect, read or collect relevant archives, materials or items. Such access is permitted on the basis of relevant national regulations and upon approval and presentation of appropriate documents. Further, state security organ personnel can also check electronic communication tools, equipment and facilities in accordance with the regulations. However, court order is not necessary when accessing archive, data, and information. Instead, Article 26 of the Law states that approval is required from the person in charge of the national security agency at the municipal level or above. In China, national security agency (国家安全机关) does not include the court.

laws: Measures for the Administration of Internet E-mail Services 2006 《互联网电子邮件服务管理办法》
impact: These measures by the MIIT provide that “Citizens’ privacy of correspondence in using Internet e-mail services shall be protected by law. Unless the public security organisation or procuratorial organisation makes an inspection on the contents of correspondence pursuant to the procedures prescribed in law when required by national security or investigation of crimes, no organisation or individual shall infringe upon any citizen’s privacy of correspondence on any pretext.” A requirement for court order is not present in the measures.

coverage: Internet service providers and telecommunication sector
laws: Counterterrorism Law of the People's Republic of China 《中华人民共和国反恐怖主义法》
impact: Article 18 of the Counterterrorism law requires Internet service providers and telecommunication sector to “provide technical support and assistance, such as technical interface and decryption, to support the activities of the public security and state security authorities in preventing and investigating terrorist activities.” In addition, no "court order" is required for the technical support and assistance.

laws: Provisions on the Management of Internet Post Comments Services 《互联网跟帖评论服务管理规定》
impact: Article 5 states that comment and reply service providers shall strictly fulfill their primary responsibilities by cooperating with relevant competent authorities in conducting supervision and inspection activities and providing the necessary technical support, documentation, and data assistance in accordance with the law. A requirement for court order is not present in the measures.

laws: Interim Administrative Measures for Generative Artificial Intelligence Services《生成式人工智能服务管理暂行办法》
impact: Article 19: Relevant regulatory authorities shall conduct supervision and inspections of generative artificial intelligence (AI) services in accordance with their responsibilities. Service providers must cooperate as required by law and provide explanations regarding the sources, scale, types, and labeling rules of training data, as well as algorithm mechanisms and principles. They must also offer necessary technical, data, and other forms of support and assistance. Institutions and personnel involved in the security assessment and supervision of generative AI services must keep confidential any state secrets, trade secrets, personal privacy, or personal information they become aware of in the course of their duties. They are prohibited from disclosing or unlawfully providing such information to others.

laws: Government of India, Ministry of Science and Technology, National Data Sharing and Accessibility Policy 2012
impact: India’s National Data Sharing and Accessibility Policy requires that “non-sensitive data available either in digital or analog forms but generated using public funds” must be stored within the borders of India. The policy states that data belongs to the "agency/department/ministry/entity which collected them and reside in their IT enabled facility.”

laws: Digital Personal Data Protection Act No. 22 2023
impact: Under chapter 4 of Special provisions: 16.(1) (Processing of personal data outside India) The Central Government may, by notification, restrict the transfer of personal data by a Data Fiduciary for processing to such country or territory outside India as may be so notified. (2) Nothing contained in this section shall restrict the applicability of any law for the time being in force in India that provides for a higher degree of protection for or restriction on transfer of personal data by a Data Fid

laws: Government of India, Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), Guidelines for Government Departments On Contractual Terms Related to Cloud Services 2015
impact: In 2015, India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MEITY) issued guidelines for a cloud computing empanelment process under which cloud computing service providers may be provisionally accredited as eligible for government procurements of cloud services. The guidelines require such providers to store all data in India to qualify for the accreditation.

laws: Reserve Bank of India Directive 2018
impact: In April 2018, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) issued a one-page directive vide circular DPSS.CO.OD.No 2785/06.08.005/2017-18 stating that, within six months, all payment data held by payment companies should be held in local facilities. The Directive noted that this would help the RBI gain "unfettered supervisory access" to transaction data, which it needs to ensure proper monitoring. Following a negative response from international payment companies such as MasterCard, Visa and American Express, the RBI has proposed (in "Frequently Asked Questions" of its website) to ease this restriction, so as to allow payment firms to store data offshore, as long as a copy was kept in India. The RBI has further clarified that for cross border transaction data consisting of a foreign component and domestic component, a copy of the domestic component may be stored abroad, if required. With respect to processing of payment transactions outside India, the RBI requires that the data must be stored only in India after processing and should be deleted from systems abroad and brought back to India no later than 24 hours after processing. Any subsequent activity such as settlement processing after payment processing done outside India, this must be undertaken on a real time basis pursuant to which the data must be stored only in India. The RBI has clarified that banks, especially foreign banks, can continue to store banking data abroad but in respect of domestic payment transactions, the data must be stored only in India.

laws: Government of India Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) No. 20(3)/2022-CERT-In Directions under sub-section (6) of section 70B of the Information Technology Act, 2000 relating to Information Security Practices, Procedure, Prevention, Response and Reporting of Cyber Incidents for Safe and Trusted Internet 2022
impact: All service providers, intermediaries, data centres, body corporate and Government organisations shall mandatorily enable logs of all their ICT systems and maintain them securely for a rolling period of 180 days and the same shall be maintained within the Indian jurisdiction (Clause vi).

laws: Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (Maintenance of Insurance Records) Regulations, 2015
Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (Outsourcing of Activities by Indian Insurers) Regulations, 2017
Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (Protection of Policyholders’ Interests, Operations and Allied Matters of Insurers) Regulations 2024
impact: According to the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) Maintenance of Insurance Records Regulations, 2015, "Insurers are required that [...] (ii) the records pertaining to policies issued and claims made in India (including the records held in electronic form) are held in data centres located and maintained in India." In addition, the 2017 Regulations on Outsourcing of Activities by Indian Insurers provide that Indian insurers, even in cases where they outsource their services outside India, must retain all original records in India. Provisions relating to outsourcing of activities have been subsumed in Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (Protection of Policyholders’ Interests, Operations and Allied Matters of Insurers) Regulations, 2024 notified on 22.03.2024. Pl refer Regulation 53(2) of the said regulation, which are reproduced hereunder. Specifically, 53 (2) In cases where insurer outsources to the service providers outside India, if permitted by the Competent Authority, the insurers shall ensure that the terms of the agreement are in compliance with respective host country regulations governing the outsourcing service provider and laws of the country concerned and such laws and regulations do not impede the regulatory access and oversight by the Authority. All original policyholder records continue to be maintained in India.

laws: Companies Act No.18 2013
impact: The Ministry of Corporate Affairs amended Section 128 of the Companies Act (2013), which requires every company to store, at its registered office, books of account, other relevant books and papers and financial statements for every financial year, to include a rule specifying all such relevant books and papers maintained in an electronic mode should remain accessible in India, at all times.

laws: Insurance Regulatory and Department Authority of India (Maintenance of Insurance Records) Regulations, 2015
impact: The records including those held in electronic mode, pertaining to all the policies issued and all claims made in India shall be held in data centres located and maintained in India only (Regulation 3(9) Maintenance of Insurance Records).

laws: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology Cyber Security Direction 2022
impact: All service providers, intermediaries, data centres, body corporate and Government organisations shall mandatorily enable logs of all their ICT systems and maintain them securely for a rolling period of 180 days and the same shall be maintained within the Indian jurisdiction (Clause iv).

laws: Digital Personal Data Protection Act No. 22 2023
impact: There are no particular requirements regarding infrastructure as of yet. Many rely on common law to settle disputes or look to the Personal Data Protection Act (2023) to follow a common practice. The Act has a Personal Data Protection Board (“the Board”), who handles consumer inquiries about the processing of their personal data, which could pretain to infrastructure, however still do not have clear mandates.

laws: Digital Personal Data Protection Act No. 22 2023
impact: Article 16 (Special provisions) of the Act states that the Central Government may, by notification, restrict the transfer of personal data by a Data Fiduciary for processing to such country or territory outside India except outside countries provides for a higher degree of protection for or restriction on transfer of personal data. The regulation also provides exemption on allowing transfer of personal data, including: (a) the processing of personal data is necessary for enforcing any legal right or claim; (b) the processing of personal data by any court or tribunal or any other body in India which is entrusted by law with the performance of any judicial or quasi-judicial or regulatory or supervisory function, where such processing is necessary for the performance of such function; (c) personal data is processed in the interest of prevention, detection, investigation or prosecution of any offence or contravention of any law for the time being in force in India; (d) personal data of Data Principals not within the territory of India is processed pursuant to any contract entered into with any person outside the territory of India by any person based in India; (e) the processing is necessary for a scheme of compromise or arrangement or merger or amalgamation of two or more companies or a reconstruction by way of demerger or otherwise of a company, or transfer of undertaking of one or more company to another company, or involving division of one or more companies, approved by a court or tribunal or other authority competent to do so by any law for the time being in force; and (f) the processing is for the purpose of ascertaining the financial information and assets and liabilities of any person who has defaulted in payment due on account of a loan or advance taken from a financial institution, subject to such processing being in accordance with the provisions regarding disclosure of information or data in any other law for the time being in force. However, this Act is not yet in force.

laws: Information Technology (Reasonable Security Practices and Procedures and Sensitive Personal Data or Information) Rules 2011
Clarification on Information Technology (Reasonable security practices and procedures and sensitive personal data or information) Rules 2011
impact: Rule 6 of the Information Technology Rules 2011 provides that cross-border data transfers of sensitive personal data or information can be made to any other corporate entity or person in India or to any other country that ensures the same level of data protection as provided under the Rules. Disclosure of sensitive personal data or information by a corporation to any third party shall require prior permission from the provider of such information, who has provided such information under lawful contract or otherwise, unless such disclosure has been agreed to in the contract between the body corporate and provider of information, or where the disclosure is necessary for compliance of a legal obligation. Sensitive personal information includes passwords, financial information such as bank account or credit/debit card details, sexual orientation, physical, mental health condition, biometric information etc. According to the Clarification on Information Technology Rules, published in August 2011, corporations providing services relating to collection, storage, dealing or handling of sensitive personal data or information under contractual obligation with any legal entity located within or outside India are not subject to the requirement of Rule 6.

laws: Digital Personal Data Protection Act No. 22 2023
impact: India's framework of data protection consists of the DPDPA (2023) "An Act to provide for the processing of digital personal data in a manner that recognises both the right of individuals to protect their personal data and the need to process such personal data for lawful purposes and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto"/ This Act focuses on safeguarding personal data by locialization of data storage, accessiblity to personal data, autonomy in how data may be used, limitations set on data fiduciaries, data processing stipulations, and over all transparency and policing. For instance, Article 4 (Grounds for processing personal data) of the Act states that a person may process the personal data of a Data Principal only in accordance with the provisions of this Act and for a lawful purpose, for which the Data Principal has given her consent or for certain legitimate uses.

laws: Master Direction on Information Technology Governance, Risk, Controls and Assurance Practices 2023
impact: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has introduced comprehensive guidelines for fintech companies ("regulated entities": RE) to ensure data protection and customer safety. RBI emphasizes the implementation of strong data protection measures, including encrypting sensitive customer data during storage and transmission (10. Third-Party Arrangements, 23. IT and Information Security Risk Management Framework, ). Under, 24. Information Security Policy and Cyber Security Policy, A senior level executive (preferably in the rank of a General Manager or an equivalent position) shall be designated as the Chief Information Security Officer (CISO). Finally, under 27. Cyber Incident Response and Recovery Management RE's cyber incident response and recovery management policy shall address the classification and assessment of incidents; include a clear communication strategy and plan to manage such incidents, contain exposures and achieve timely recovery.

laws: Government of India, Ministry of Communication and Information Technology, National Cyber Security Policy 2013
impact: The vision of this policy is "To build a secure and resilient cyberspace for citizens , businesses and Government". The policy gives a framework to create a secure, resilient cyberspace. It also talks about strategies to do so,strengthening of regulatory framework (section D) to develop a dynamic legal frameowkr to address cybersecurity challenges arising out of technological developments in the cyber space, early warning systems (section E) especially at the national level, response to threats etc.

laws: Information Technology Act No.21 2000
impact: While its not solely focused on cybersecurity, there are some sections that do provide a framework to deal with cyberthreats. Example, Chapter 9 mentions penalties for cybercrimes and Chapter 11 mentions offences in the cyberspace like tampering source codes, hacking, publishing obscene information. Specifically, Article 65 prescribes that whoever knowingly or intentionally conceals, destroys or alters or intentionally or knowingly causes another to conceal, destroy or alter any computer source code used for a computer, computer programme, computer system or computer network, when the computer source code is required to be kept or maintained by law for the time being in force, shall be punishable with imprisonment up to three years, or with fine which may extend up to two lakh rupees, or with both. "Computer source code" means the listing of programmes, computer commands, design and layout and programme analysis of computer resource in any form.

laws: Master Direction on Information Technology Governance, Risk, Controls and Assurance Practices 2023
impact: In chapter 4, section 24, the guidelines outline a cybersecurity policy: regulated entities (REs) shall also put in place a Cyber Security Policy and Cyber Crisis Management Plan (CCMP).

laws: Comprehensive Cyber Security Framework for Primary (Urban) Cooperative Banks (UCBs) – A Graded Approach 2019
impact: This document outlines security controls for cooperative banks, with a focus on data security and encryption to prevent cyber-attacks. For instance under "Baseline Cyber Security and Resilience Requirements - Level I" banks muts implement specific email domains, two factor authentication, security reviews and robust password management. Under additional requirements, banks are also required to have network management and must conduct "Vulnerability Assessment/ Penetration Testing (VA/PT)"

laws: Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations 2015
impact: As per the SEBI Listing Regulations, a listed entity (i.e. an entity which is listed on the stock market) is required to have a policy for the preservation of documents. The SEBI Listing Regulations require that records, books, papers and documents of the company be preserved as per the following classifications: i) Schedule I - to be preserved permanently. Documents listed under these schedule include incorporation documents, share certificates, register of minutes of board meetings, register of members etc. ii) Schedule II – to be preserved for eight years. Documents listed under this schedule include books of accounts, attendance register of board meetings, register of debenture holders etc. iii) Schedule III – to be preserved for a minimum period of five years or such higher period as may be determine by the board of directors of the company. Documents listed under this schedule include register of stock options, register of directors and key managerial personnel, disclosures made under applicable company laws etc. As per the SEBI Listing Regulations, documents set out in Schedule I and II can be kept in electronic mode. The complete list of documents under each schedule is set out in the SEBI Listing Regulations.

impact: Due diligence by an intermediary: An intermediary, including a social media intermediary, a significant social media intermediary and an online gaming intermediary, shall observe the following due diligence while discharging its duties, namely: (g) where upon receiving actual knowledge under clause (d), on a voluntary basis on violation of clause (b), or on the basis of grievances received under sub-rule (2) any information has been removed or access to which has been disabled, the intermediary shall, without vitiating the evidence in any manner, preserve such information and associated records for one hundred and eighty days for investigation purposes, or for such longer period as may be required by the court or by Government agencies who are lawfully authorised; (h) where an intermediary collects information from a user for registration on the computer resource, it shall retain his information for a period of one hundred and eighty days after any cancellation or withdrawal of his registration, as the case may be.
