laws: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Market Infrastructure Institutions) Regulations 2021
Securities Contracts (Regulation) Rules, 1957
impact: Regulation 39(1) of IFSCA (Market Infrastructure Institutions) Regulations, 2021 and Rule 14 of the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Rules, 1957 requires that stock exchanges must keep the following books and records in an electronic retrieval form for minimum of 20 years: (1) Minute books of the meetings of— (a) members; (b) governing body; (c) any standing committee or committees of the governing body or of the general body of members. (2) Register of members showing their full names and addresses. Where any member of the stock exchange is a firm, full names and addresses of all partners shall be shown. (3)Register of authorised clerks. (4)Register of remisiers of authorised assistants. (5)Record of security deposits. (6)Margin deposits book. (7)Ledgers. (8)Journals. (9)Cash book. (10)Bank passbook (11) such other records as may be specified by Authority from time to time. Regulation 39(2) of the Regulation, every recognized clearing corporation shall maintain and preserve the following documents in electronic retrieval form (minimum period of 20 years): (a) Minute books of the meetings of: (i) governing board; (ii) any committees of the governing board; (b) Record of clearing members showing their full names, addresses and details of bank and depository accounts for settlement purposes; (c) Transaction records; (d) Record of security deposits; (e) Margin deposits book; (f) Client margin collection details; (g) Ledgers; (h) Journals; (i) Cash book; (j) Bank account statement; (k) Such other records as may be specified by the Authority from time to time. Additionally, regulation 57 of the Regulation, every recognized depository shall maintain the following documents in electronic retrieval form (a minimum period of 20 years): a) records of securities dematerialised and rematerialised; b) the names of the transferor, transferee, and the dates of transfer of securities; c) a register and an index of beneficial owners; d) details of the holding of the securities of beneficial owners as at the end of each day; e) records of instructions received from and sent to participants, issuers, issuers’ agents and beneficial owners; f) records of approval, notice, entry and cancellation of pledge or hypothecation, as the case may be; g) details of participants; h) details of securities declared to be eligible for dematerialisation in the depository; and i) such other records as may be specified by the Authority from time to time.

laws: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations 2021
impact: Regulation 14(1) of IFSCA Capital Market Intermediaries Regulation, every capital market intermediary shall maintain the following books and records in electronic retrieval form ( a minimum period of 10 years): a) a copy of the balance sheet at the end of each accounting period; b) a copy of profit and loss account for each accounting period; c) a copy of the auditor’s report on the accounts for each accounting period; d) a statement of net worth for each quarter; e) documentation relating to compliance with AML and CFT guidelines; f) documents relating to account opening of each client and any power of attorney or signature authority forms of the clients; g) relevant records and documents relating to its activities in capital markets; and h) such other books of accounts, records and documents as may be specified by the Authority from time to time. Regulation 14(2) of the Regulations, in relation to a capital market intermediary not being a body corporate, it shall maintain the following books of accounts in electronic retrieval from a minimum peiord of 10 years, records and documents, namely, - (a) all sums of money received and expended; (b) its assets and liabilities; (c) a statement of net worth for each quarter; (d) documentation relating to compliance with AML and CFT guidelines; (e) documents relating to account opening of each client and any power of attorney or signature authority forms of the clients; (f) relevant records and documents relating to its activities in capital markets; and (g) such other books of accounts, record and documents as may be specified by the Authority from time to time.

laws: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Fund Management) Regulations 2022
impact: Regulation 119(2) of the IFSCA (Fund Management) Regulations 2022, every Fund Management Entity shall maintain the following records for a minimum period of 10 years in electronic retrieval form: a) a copy of the balance sheet at the end of each accounting period; b) a copy of profit and loss account for each accounting period; c) a copy of the auditor’s report on the accounts for each accounting period; d) a statement of net worth for each quarter; e) documents relating to compliance with AML and CFT guidelines; f) documents relating to account opening of each client and any power of attorney or signature authority forms of the clients; g) relevant records and documents relating to its activities under these regulations; and h) such other books of accounts, records and documents as may be specified by the Authority from time to time. Additionally, Regulation 119(3), every Fund Management Entity shall maintain the following records in electronic retrieval form (a minimum period of 5 years after the winding up of the scheme): a) the assets under each scheme; b) valuation policies and practices; c) investment strategies; d) particulars of investors and their contribution; e) rationale for investments made.

laws: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Maintenance of Insurance Records and Submission of Requisite Information for Investigation and Inspection) Regulations 2022
impact: In terms of Regulation 10 of IFSCA (Maintenance of Insurance Records and Submission of Requisite Information for Investigation and Inspection) Regulations 2022, every IIO and IIIO shall maintain all records, information, data, documents, books and registers maintained under the Insurance Act, 1938, any other applicable law or the rules, regulations, guidelines, circulars or directions issued thereunder. For a minimum period of 7 years, as prescribed under clause (8) of rule 39 of the Insurance Rules, 1939, or as per other applicable legal requirements, whichever is later. The period shall be counted from the date – a) of last transaction on the respective records or from the date of expiry of the policy whichever is later; b) on which the claim is settled.”

laws: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Anti Money Laundering, Counter Terrorist-Financing and Know Your Customer) Guidelines 2022
impact: In terms of Clause 9 of IFSCA (Anti Money Laundering, Counter Terrorist Financing and Know Your Customer Guidelines 2022), all Regulated Entities shall maintain the following records: (a) a copy of all documents and information obtained in undertaking initial and ongoing Customer Due Diligence; (b) records of customer business relationships (both original and certified copies), which include: - (i) correspondence of business and other information relating to a customer’s account; (ii) adequate records of transactions to enable standalone transactions to be reconstructed; and (iii) internal findings and analysis relating to a business transaction or other transactions, where the transaction or business may be unusual or suspicious, whether or not it results in a Suspicious Transactions Report; (c) notifications made under Clause 10.1.(b) of the Guidelines [Policies, procedures, systems and controls, put up in place by the Regulated Entities, which ensure that whenever any of its employee, acting in the ordinary course of his employment, either: (i) knows; (ii) suspects; or (iii) has reasonable grounds for knowing or suspecting; that a person is engaged in or attempting ML/TF, that employee promptly notifies the Principal Officer of the Regulated Entity with all relevant details].; (d) Suspicious Transactions Reports and any relevant supporting documents and information, including internal findings and analysis; (e) any relevant communications, if made with the FIU; (f) all the risk assessment documents referred to in Clause 9.4 of the Guidelines; and (g) any other matter that the Regulated Entity may be expressly required to record and maintain, under these Guidelines. For a minimum period of 6 years at least six years or for such period as prescribed under the applicable laws, from the date on which business relationship has ended or transaction is completed.

laws: International Financial Services Centres Authority Banking Handbook on Conduct of Business Directions 2023
impact: Module No.3 (clause 6) of the Banking Handbook: Banks shall keep records of: (a) the procedures which it has followed under this module including any documents that evidence the Client’s classification; and (b) any notification sent to the Client under module, together with evidence of dispatch. At least seven years from the date on which the business relationship with a client ended or for such period as may be required by any law, whichever is longer. Module No.4 (clause 7) of the Banking Handbook: An Authorised Promoter must keep a record of all Communications with clients Financial Promotion that it makes or approves. The record must include at least the following detail: (a) the name of the senior Employee who reviewed the Financial Promotion; (b) the date the Financial Promotion was made or approved; (c) if the Financial Promotion was in writing, a copy of the Financial Promotion; and (d) if the Financial Promotion was not in writing, details of the Financial Promotion and its outcome, including a note stating if the Client requested the termination of a real time Financial Promotion. The Authorised Promoter must keep the records for at least 7 years after the Financial Promotion is no longer made or for such period as may be required by any law, whichever is longer. Note: the records should contain the name of the complainant, the substance of the complaint, a record of the BU’s response, and any other relevant correspondence or records, and the action taken by the IBU to resolve each complaint. A minimum period of seven years from the date of receipt of a complaint or the period mandated by any law, whichever is longer. Module No.13 of the Banking Handbook: An IFSC Covered Entity should ensure that all relevant books, and all transaction information and related information are kept – (a) in the case of any relevant book, until at least five years after the last date of the expiry or termination of a contract, an agreement or a transaction to which the book relates; (b) in the case of any transaction information or related information until at least five years after the date of the expiry or termination of the contract, agreement or transaction to which the information relates.

laws: Companies Act No.18 2013

laws: Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules 2021
impact: Under the Information Technology Rules of 2021, a "significant" social media intermediary (defined as a social media intermediary having number of registered users in India above 5,000,000) must appoint a Chief Compliance Officer who must ensure compliance with the Rules and will be liable in any proceedings relating to any relevant third-party information, data or communication link made available or hosted by that intermediary where he/she fails to ensure that such intermediary observes due diligence while discharging its duties under the Rules (Rule 4 Additional due diligence to be observed by significant social media intermediary and online gaming intermediary).

laws: Digital Personal Data Protection Act No. 22 2023

laws: Information Technology Act No.21 2000
impact: Section 69 (Power to issue directions for interception or monitoring or decryption of any information through any computer resource) of the Information Technology Act 2000, as amended by the Information Technology (Amendment) Act 2008, gives the central and state governments the power to direct any agency to intercept, monitor or decrypt, or cause to be intercepted, monitored or decrypted any information transmitted, received or stored through any computer resources. The government may require any subscriber or intermediary or any person in charge of the computer resource to extend all facilities and technical assistance necessary to decrypt the information. laws: Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Interception, Monitoring and Decryption of Information) Rules 2009
impact: The Rules provide that the officer so designated by the Central Government under the Rules (known as 'Designated Officer') can on the receipt of request from any nodal officer of a government organisation or a competent court or by an order of any agency of the government can block access by the public to any information transmitted, received, stored or hosted in any computer resource. laws: Law No.27 on Personal Data Protection 2022
impact: Indonesia's approach to cross-border data policies is primarily governed by the Personal Data Protection Law (PDP Law), which was enacted in 2022 and is set to be fully enforced by October 2024. The Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) of 2022 is Indonesia’s first comprehensive law dedicated specifically to personal data protection. It significantly updates and consolidates personal data governance compared to Law No. 11 of 2008 on Electronic Information and Transactions (EIT Law) and Government Regulation No. 82 of 2012 (Regulation 82). The PDPA does not fully replace the EIT Law or Regulation 82, but it supersedes and updates many of their provisions related to data privacy, creating a more robust framework for data protection. Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA), 2022 does not mandate strict localization but emphasizes secure data transfer practices. Under Article 55, the PDPA allows cross-border data transfers but imposes conditions to ensure that the data is protected according to Indonesian standards. Transfers are allowed if the destination country has an equivalent level of data protection, or contractual safeguards are in place to protect the data. Article 56 states that the Data Controller may transfer personal data to other Data Controllers and/or Data Processors outside the jurisdiction of the Republic of Indonesia in accordance with the provisions regulated in this law. It emphasizes that when transferring personal data, the Data Controller must ensure that the country where the receiving Data Controller and/or Data Processor is located provides an adequate level of personal data protection. If the level of protection is not adequate, the Data Controller must ensure that there are adequate and binding safeguards in place. If neither condition is met, explicit consent from the data subject must be obtained for the transfer. Article 66 addresses requirements for data security and confidentiality, essential for sectors handling sensitive data, like banking and finance, mandating that personal data be processed securely to protect against unauthorized access. Articles 65 and 67 prohibit unauthorized collection, disclosure, or usage of personal data, establishing penalties for non-compliance, which directly affects financial service providers’ handling of customer data. Article 74 of transitional Provisions states that existing data controllers and processors must comply with the new law within two years of its enactment (October 2024), allowing time for organizations to adjust their practices.

The Government Regulation No. 40 of 2019 further clarifies the definition of personal data to be protected that include fingerprint, signature, iris (in eyes), disgraces, notes on mental or physical diseases. Moreover, Law No. 27 establishes a general framework for the protection of personal data in Indonesia. It is closely aligned with international data privacy standards, and is largely modelled on the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation. Data controllers, data processors and relevant parties that process personal data are given a two year transition period following the enactment of Law No. 27, thus up to 17 October 2024 to conform with it. Once the transition period elapses, all such parties must comply with all the provisions of Law No. 27 and any noncompliance thereto may possibly be enforced. Indonesia enacted the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) of 2022, establishing Indonesia’s first dedicated and comprehensive data protection framework, akin to international standards like the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Key features of the PDPA include: 1. Clear Definition of Personal Data and Comprehensive Rights for Data Subjects: Article 6: Grants data subjects the right to correct and update their data. Article 8: Provides the right to request the deletion or termination of processing personal data. Article 9: Allows withdrawal of consent for data processing. Article 11: Allows data subjects to limit or suspend the processing of their data 2. Cross-Border Transfer Rules: Allows data transfers abroad under strict conditions, ensuring equivalent protection. Article 55: Governs cross-border transfers, permitting them only if the destination country has adequate protection measures or appropriate safeguards are in place 3. Data Processing Obligations: Imposes duties on data controllers and processors for secure and lawful data handling. Article 35: Requires data controllers to implement organizational and technical measures to ensure data protection. Article 39: Mandates appointment of a Data Protection Officer (DPO) for entities processing sensitive data or conducting large-scale processing. Articles 40–42: Specify reporting obligations in case of data breaches, ensuring accountability and transparency 4. Enforcement and Penalties: Provides for administrative sanctions and criminal penalties for violations. Article 67: Imposes administrative fines for non-compliance. Articles 66–68: Stipulate criminal penalties for unauthorized access, misuse, or other breaches of personal data However, the PDPA is still being operationalized and will fully come into effect in October 2024, alongside sector-specific regulations (e.g., financial and health) that augment its application. impact: Law No. 11 of 2008 on Information and Electronic Transactions (ITE Law) has been amended by Law No. 19 of 2016 and further revised through the Second Amendment by Law No. 1 of 2024. Government Regulation No. 71 of 2019 on the Implementation of Electronic Systems and Transactions (PP 71/2019), which implements the ITE Law, specifies in Article 40(2) that electronic system providers must retain electronic records for at least 5 years.

laws: Bank Indonesia Regulation No. 22/23/PBI/2020 on Payment Systems 2020
Regulation of Financial Services Authority No.11/POJK.03/2022 on the Implementation of Information Technology by Commercial Banks 2022
Law No.10 on Banking 1998

Regulation of Financial Services Authority No. LN.2023 (11)/117 on on the Implementation of Anti-Money Laundering (AML) Programs, Prevention of Terrorism Financing, and Prevention of Financing for the Proliferation of Weapons of Mass Destruction (WMD) in the Financial Services Sector 2023
impact: In relation to data retention obligations in the Banking sector, data retention can be adjusted to the needs and policies of each Bank. However, OJK views the retention period as one of the important indicators in the IT risk management framework, as stated in the Financial Services Authority Circular Letter No. 29/SEOJK.03/2022 concerning Cyber Resilience and Security for Commercial Banks, where the data retention period is one of the assessment pillars in the asset protection process parameters that reflect the implementation of data and information security management, as well as data management in line with cybersecurity-related risk management to protect the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data and information. Bank Indonesia Regulation No. 22/23/PBI/2020 on Payment Systems: - Article 35(3) requires payment service providers (PJP) to process payment transactions domestically and retain transaction data for compliance and audit purposes. While the regulation does not explicitly state a minimum retention period, it is implied that data must be retained for as long as necessary to meet regulatory and operational requirements. OJK Regulation No. 11/POJK.03/2022 on IT Implementation by Banks: - Article 43(1) requires banks to manage data effectively to support business objectives, but it does not specify a minimum retention period. However, Article 54(4) mandates that banks conduct internal audits of IT systems at least once a year, which implies that data must be retained for at least one year to support these audits. Law No. 10 of 1998 on Banking - The Law No. 10 of 1998 on Banking does not specifically state that Banks are required to retain customer transaction data for at least 5 years after the account is closed. However, art. 21 para (2) of Law Number 8 of 2010 on the Prevention and Eradication of Money Laundering Crimes regulates that Reporting Parties are required to retain records and documents related to the identity of parties conducting transactions for a minimum of 5 years after the termination of the business relationship. In the context of Law No. 8 of 2010, Reporting Parties includes, among others, banks as one of the financial service providers. Law No.8/2023 on on the Implementation of Anti-Money Laundering (AML) Programs, Prevention of Terrorism Financing, and Prevention of Financing for the Proliferation of Weapons of Mass Destruction (WMD) in the Financial Services - Article 63 para 1 regulates that Financial Service Providers (FSPs) are obligated to retain documents related to prospective customers, customers, or walk-in customers for at least 5 years after the end of the business relationship or the discovery of irregular transactions. Additionally, documents related to financial transactions must be stored in accordance with company documentation regulations.

laws: Law No.27 on Personal Data Protection 2022
impact: Indonesia's Personal Data Protection Act (Law No. 27 of 2022) and the Minister of Communication and Informatics Regulation No. 20 of 2016 establish that DPO and DPIA requirement, applied to all sectors: DPO Requirement in Article 53 of Law No. 27 of 2022 that mandates that data controllers and processors appoint a DPO under specific circumstances, which can apply across various sectors, particularly when: - The processing is for public services. - The nature, scope, and purposes of the processing require organized and systematic supervision on a large scale. - The processing involves large-scale processing of specific data or data related to criminal conduct. DPIA Requirement in Article 34 of Law No. 27 of 2022, which states that data controllers must conduct a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) if the processing poses a high potential risk to data subjects. This requirement is applicable across all sectors where high-risk processing occurs, such as: - Automatic decision-making with legal consequences. - Processing of specific personal data. - Large-scale processing of personal data. - Systematic evaluation, scoring, or monitoring of data subjects.

laws: Regulation of the Minister of Communication and Informatics of the Republic of Indonesia No.20 on Protection of Personal Data in Electronic Systems 2016
impact: According to Article 34 of Law No. 27, the data controller is obliged to conduct a Data Protection Impact Assessment if the personal data processing has a high potential risk to the personal data subjects. Personal data processing with high potential risk includes: - automatic decision-making that has legal consequences or a significant impact on the data subject; - processing of specific personal data; - processing of large-scale personal data; - processing of personal data for systematic evaluation, scoring, or monitoring of data subjects; - processing of personal data for the activity of matching or combining a group of data; - the use of new technologies in the processing of personal data; and/or - the processing of personal data that limits the exercise of the rights of the data subject. The Minister of Communication and Informatics Regulation No. 20 of 2016 mandates the electronic system operators to have a contact person that can be contacted by the data owner for them to make inquiries about their data protection.

laws: Regulation of the Government of the Republic of Indonesia No.71 on the Provision of Electronic System and Transaction 2019

laws: Law No.17 on State Intelligence 2011

impact: The Law on State Intelligence passed in October 2011 mandates that the collection of information on a person, that is considered harmful to national interest and security, should be based on the Head of State Intelligence Agency's order. The Law broadly authorizes the Indonesian State Intelligence Agency (BIN) to engage in eﬀorts “to prevent and/or to fight any eﬀort, work, intelligence activity, and/or opponents that may be harmful to national interests and national security” (Article 6). This may include communications surveillance. BIN's intelligence activities, including to collect information, should meet the following requirements: 1) they are for the purpose of intelligence function; 2) they are based on Head of BIN's order; 3) they should be conducted without making any arrest and/or detention; and 4) they should be conducted in a cooperation with law enforcement agency. Civil society advocates in Indonesia had denounced the draft bill, which was nevertheless passed. The Minister of Communication and Informatics Regulation No. 20 of 2016 allows the government to access the electronic personal data for investigation purposes by law enforcement officers.

Law on Electronic Transactions No.20/NA 2010
impact: Lao PDR does not implement ban to transfer and requirement to process data locally. The definition of data processing is provided and to process data, the data controller must obtain a data subject's consent. The law does not enforce a strict local processing mandate but rather sets forth a series of conditions that must be met before data can be processed or transferred, particularly abroad. It focuses on security measures, such as encryption and consent, rather than requiring that all data processing must remain within the country.

The Law on Electronic Data Protection and the Law on Electronic Transactions in Lao PDR do not currently enforce an explicit infrastructure data localization requirement across all sectors. However, there are key provisions that emphasize ensuring secure systems and adequate data safeguards, especially for sensitive and critical data.

laws: Law on Electronic Data Protection No.25/NA 2017
impact: The Law on Electronic Data Protection specifies that the delivery or transfer of data must be performed as follows: - with the consent of the data subject and guarantee that the transferee can protect such data; - with the encryption of important information, such as financial, accounting, and investment data and with the electronic certificate issued by the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunication (Article 25); - without forging the source of data sent or transferred; - that the transfer must be in accordance with the agreement of the transferee and transferor; and - that the transfer must be stopped upon refusal by transferee. The scope of the Law on Electronic Data Protection (2017) primarily covers the protection of personal data and other sensitive data. Specifically, Article 2 (Definitions) and Article 4 (Scope of Application) provide insights into the applicability: - Article 2 defines personal data as any information relating to an individual, which can be used directly or indirectly to identify that person. -Article 4 clarifies that the law applies to personal data and the management, processing, and storage of such data by both public and private sector entities within Lao PDR. This includes ensuring appropriate levels of security and confidentiality for handling personal data. The law, therefore, explicitly focuses on the protection of personal data and outlines measures for safeguarding the privacy of individuals, without extending to all categories of non-personal or generic data. - Article 10: Defines sensitive data as information that cannot be accessed, used, or disclosed without the consent of the Information Owner. This includes information on financials, health, personal data, etc. -Article 11: Outlines the responsibilities of the Data Administrator, including ensuring that sensitive data is adequately protected. -Article 15: Requires periodic risk assessments, backup systems, and other measures to safeguard sensitive data. Specifies requirements for protecting sensitive data, including ensuring secure storage and conducting annual risk assessments. - Article 16: Addresses encryption requirements for transferring sensitive data, specifically mentioning that important documents (e.g., financial, banking, and investment data) must be encrypted during cross-border transfers. The transfer of private data outside of Lao PDR is subject to the express consent of data subject and compliance with law (Article 17 Sending or Transferring of Electronic Data).

laws: Decree on the Financial Consumer Protection No. 225/GOL 2020
impact: There is no specific mention in the documents regarding conditional flow regimes for all sectors. However, there are provisions and requirements for specific types of data, mainly sensitive data and financial data, that must be handled with extra security measures. Sensitive data (e.g., financial, medical, customer information) must be handled with explicit consent from the data owner and must be encrypted when being transferred, especially across borders. Additionally, the Decree on Consumer Protection Concerning Financial Services, which ensures that financial institutions must protect customer data and may not transfer sensitive financial information without proper safeguards. - Article 21: Ensures that financial institutions take responsibility for collecting and handling customer information with transparency, including obtaining consent. - Article 30: Discusses provisions to protect sensitive financial information and customer data, ensuring financial institutions implement proper safeguards for transferring data.

laws: Law on Electronic Data Protection No.25/NA 2017
Guidelines on the Implementation of the Law on Electronic Data Protection No. 2126/MoPTC
impact: Lao PDR does not have comprehensive data protection law. The data protection in Lao PDR mainly refers to the protection of data in electronic format. The protection can be found in specific regulations, such as the Law on Electronic Data Protection No.25/NA, Law on Prevention and Combating Cybercrime No. 61/NA, and Penal Code No. 26/NA. Specifically, under the Electronic Data Protection No. 25/NA, the electronic data refers to general data (data of individual, legal entities or organizations) and specific data (official/personal data that not allow individual, legal entities or organizations to access, use or disclose without permission from the owner or relevant organizations) (Articles 8-10). Additionally, in August 2018, to clarify the requirements under the Law on Electronic Data Protection, the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications issued the Guidelines on the Implementation of the Law on Electronic Data Protection No. 2126/MoPTC. The E-Data Protection Guidelines provide greater clarity on the classification of electronic data, the compliance obligations of data managers, and rules associated with regulated data protection activities. These Guidelines cover: (i) data collection; (ii) electronic data inspection; (iii) saving/storing of electronic data; (iv) maintaining electronic data; (v) using and disseminating electronic data; (vi) transmission and transfer of electronic data; (vii) access to electronic data; (viii) amending and updating electronic data; and (ix) deletion of electronic data. Lao PDR has no comprehensive data protection framework that applies universally across all sectors. Instead, the country has adopted a more sector-specific (sectoral) approach to data protection. The Law on Electronic Data Protection (2017) does provide guidelines for the handling and processing of sensitive data, such as personal, financial, and medical information, but these rules are often integrated into other sectoral regulations. Lao PDR is still in the process of developing a more robust data protection regime, with ongoing efforts to enhance the legal and institutional framework for data security​ (ESCAP-2022-PB-Readiness)​ (Implementation Guide). However, the country has not yet enacted a comprehensive, cross-sectoral data protection law similar to the GDPR or California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA), which would apply universally across all sectors.

laws: Law on Prevention and Combating Cyber Crime No.61/NA 2015
impact: Lao PDR does have a dedicated cybersecurity legal framework, though it is somewhat sector-specific rather than being a comprehensive, horizontal framework that applies across all sectors. The Law on Prevention and Combating Cyber Crime (2015) provides a foundation for cybersecurity in Lao PDR. This law establishes principles, regulations, and measures for managing and monitoring cybersecurity efforts, including the protection of computer systems, data, and information​. The law focuses on cybercrime, detailing offenses like unauthorized access, data forgery, and system interference. Article 6 (Scope of the law enforcement), applies to person, legal entity, and organizations both domestic and foreign living and resarching and operating computer system and computer's data and inforamtion in Lao PDR. Also Article 3 (Definitions), the term 'personal data and information' refers to any data and information. Although the law provides a dedicated legal framework for cybersecurity, it primarily focuses on criminal aspects of cyber threats rather than encompassing a broad, horizontal cybersecurity strategy that applies to all sectors, including critical infrastructure, public sector entities, and private industries. Additionally, sectoral regulations, like those for telecommunications, further address cybersecurity concerns in specific areas.

laws: Law on Electronic Transactions No.20/NA 2010
impact: The language used in the Law on Electronic Transactions (2012), specifically in Article 16, states that individuals, legal entities, or organizations "may store" documents electronically, which implies that electronic storage is an option rather than a mandatory requirement. This means that the law provides the flexibility to retain documents electronically, but it does not impose a strict, mandatory minimum retention period across all sectors.

laws: Law on Electronic Data Protection No.25/NA 2017
impact: There are no explicit minimum data retention periods mentioned in the Law on Electronic Data Protection (2017). However, the law requires that data controllers (organizations responsible for managing data) ensure the security and integrity of data they collect and store. This responsibility implies that data controllers must maintain data as long as necessary to fulfill their obligations under national laws, but no specific period is outlined.

laws: Law on Prevention and Combating Cyber Crime No.61/NA 2015
impact: Law on Prevention and Combating Cyber Crime No. 61/NA (2015) specifies that service providers must retain computer traffic data for a minimum period. According to Article 40 (Prohibitions for Service Providers) of the law, service providers are prohibited from deleting computer traffic data for a minimum of 90 days if they have a connection system, and 365 days if they do not. Implying that service providers are expected to monitor users' data to some extent and provide it to authorities when requested. This ensures that the data is available for legal or investigative purposes, particularly in cybercrime investigations. The law allows authorities to monitor, inspect, and take necessary actions regarding online content that violates national security or public order​.

laws: Law on Electronic Data Protection No.25/NA 2017
impact: There is a general obligation for a data processor or controller to maintain staff for data security administration under the Law. The Law does not explicitly state the requirements of a data protection officer ('DPO') for administrators. Articles 29 and 30 states that data controller has the right and obligation to establish an internal department and officer to supervise the protection of the data. Article 46 also mandates that the content of inspection of electronic data protection should include the responsibilities, behavior, and working methodologies of Electronic Data Protection officers. However, there is no clarification to what that roles and its responsibilities entail.

laws: Law on Electronic Data Protection No.25/NA 2017
impact: The Law on Electronic Data Protection (2017) includes provisions that allow government access to personal data under specific conditions, primarily for reasons related to national security, public order, or in the case of legal proceedings. Electronic Data Administration Authorities (Article 3) refers to individual, legal entities, or organizations that responsible for administrating the electronic data which mainly are Ministries, Data Center through internet, telecom services providers, and banks. According to the law, personal data may be accessed or disclosed by government authorities if it aligns with the needs of public safety or legal requirements. For instance, Article 14 of the law emphasizes that the protection of personal data must be balanced with the need to maintain national security and stability. The authority has the right to intercept the electronic data that effect on the stability of the nation, peace and orderliness of the society (Article 29 Rights of the Data Administration Authority, Clause 1). However, the authority require to request permission from data owner. It is prohibited to access, use, collect, disclose, or disseminate electronic data without permission (Articles 30 Obligation of data administration authority and 33 Prohibition for the Data Administration Authority).

laws: Law on Prevention and Combating Cyber Crime No.61/NA 2015
impact: The Cybercrime Law does mention that government authorities can access and retain certain types of data for investigations under specific conditions, particularly in the context of cybercrime. Article 40 of the Cybercrime Law prohibits service providers from deleting certain data, like computer traffic data, within a specific retention period unless instructed by relevant authorities. Article 45 allows for emergency investigation measures where authorities may access computer data to prevent imminent threats or cybercrimes. Therefore, while there are cases where government authorities may gain access to data, it is generally part of an established legal process rather than unrestricted access without judicial oversight.

impact: Article 3 (Technological safety requirements) of the "Regulation on Technical Requirements for Processing Sensitive, Biometric, and Genetic Data" sets out the requirements for servers processing sensitive personal information. The data processing server must meet the following requirements: 3.2.1. Be located in the territory of Mongolia; 3.2.2. be accessible only from Mongolia; 3.2.3. The server must be located in a dedicated technical room; 3.2.4. Ability to increase server capacity if necessary; 3.2.5. The data processor shall have a firewall system that regularly monitors incoming and outgoing network traffic and blocks suspicious activity and access in order to ensure network security. Pursuant to Article 1, the objective of this Regulation is to establish the principles and technological security requirements governing the processing of sensitive personal data, as well as genetic and biometric data, as stipulated in Articles 9 and 10 of the Law on the Protection of Personal Data.

impact: The purpose of this law is to regulate relations pertaining to establishing the system, principles, and legal framework in ensuring cyber security, and ensuring the safety, confidentiality, and accessibility of information within cyberspace and cyber environments. laws: Law on Personal Data Protection
impact: Mongolia does not mandate DPO or DPIA requirement. As stipulated in Article 22.2, should the breach impact the rights and legal interests of the data owner, the data controller must promptly notify the data owner. The data owner is empowered, following Article 22.4, to file a complaint with the relevant authorities if they believe their rights and legal interests have been violated, as elaborated in Article 22.2 of this law. laws: Banking Law of Mongolia
impact: Article 7.2 of the law mandates that shareholders, the chairperson of the board of directors, members, executive management, review board, and employees of the bank must refrain from disclosing, revealing, or using any information considered confidential by the bank, its customers, or third parties, except in the following circumstances: - The individual must provide written consent to disclose the Information; laws: Federal Law No. 152-FZ “On Personal Data”
impact: The primary legislative instrument of data protection in Russia is the Federal Law No. 152-FZ "On Personal Data". Article 1. Scope of Application of this Federal Law 1.1 This Federal Law regulates relations associated with the processing of personal data carried out by: - Federal government authorities, - Authorities of the constituent entities of the Russian Federation, - Other state bodies (hereinafter — state authorities), - Local self-government bodies, - Other municipal authorities (hereinafter — municipal authorities), - Legal entities, and - Individuals using automation tools, including those operating via information and telecommunication networks, or without the use of such tools, if the nature of the actions (operations) performed on the personal data without automation tools corresponds to those typically performed using such tools. impact: In addition to comprehensive legislation that applies horizontally across all sectors, the Russian Federation has also developed and implemented a wide range of sector-specific regulations related to data protection, offering detailed guidance tailored to different industries. Some of these sectoral laws are listed below: Chapter 14 of the Federal Law on the Labour Code of the Russian Federation focuses on the protection of employees’ personal data. It sets out a series of provisions ranging from general requirements for processing and safeguarding personal data to rules on its storage and transfer. Chapter 12 of the Federal Law on the Fundamentals of Health Protection of Citizens in the Russian Federation contains specific provisions for handling healthcare-related personal data, including requirements for a unified state information system in the field of healthcare. In addition, laws such as the Federal Law on Advertising and the Federal Law on Banks and Banking Activities also include very few dedicated provisions on information and data governance.

impact: Russia tends not to use the idiom of 'cybersecurity' in its official legal documents. In Russia cybersecurity is an integral part of the information security concept. Information security is quite broadly defined and understood as protection of an individual, society and/or the state against internal and external information threats, thereby maintaining the constitutional rights and freedoms, and quality and standard of living of citizens, as well as the sovereignty, territorial integrity and sustainable socio-economic development of the Russian Federation, and the defence and security of the state. Therefore, in Russia cybersecurity is understood as one of the elements of information security, i.e., cybersecurity requirements are implemented in the context of the information security policy. In 2014, the Russian business community attempted to alter the country’s approach to cybersecurity: a national cybersecurity strategy was proposed whereunder businesses and civil society would participate in the development of the cybersecurity standards and policy, international cooperation in cybersecurity would increase and other states’ experience would be implemented. However, the strategy was criticised by the RF Federal Security Service (FSS) and was never adopted. Instead the Information Security Doctrine of the Russian Federation was adopted two years later (the Russian Federation No. 646 On Adopting the Doctrine of Information Security). It does not provide for the business community’s participation in development of cybersecurity standards, but sets out broad principles, such as protection of constitutional rights, protection of Russia’s critical information infrastructure, development of Russian science and IT, delivery of accurate information on Russian state policy and official positions to domestic society and internationally, assistance in the creation of an international information security system, and protection of Russian sovereignty in the information field. Moreover, regulations such as the Federal Law on Personal Data include provisions that are generally considered cybersecurity measures. For instance, the law imposes additional cybersecurity reporting requirements on entities that collect personal data. Specifically, Article 21 requires personal data operators to report any cyberattacks or unauthorized data transmissions to the relevant authorities within 24 hours of the incident and to inform them of the measures taken to mitigate potential harm to data subjects resulting from the breach.

impact: According to Section 28, Part 3 (Use or Disclosure of Personal Data) of the Personal Data of the Personal Data Protection Act 2019 (PDPA), transferring data outside Thailand is only allowed if the destination country has adequate data protection standards or approaches. Specifically, the event that the Data Controller sends or transfers the personal data to a foreign country, the destination country or international organization that receives such personal data shall have adequate data protection standard, and shall be carried out in accordance with the rules for the protection of personal data as prescribed by the Committee in section 16(5), except in the following circumstances: (1) where it is for compliance with the law; (2) where the consent of the data subject has been obtained, provided that the data subject has been informed of the inadequate personal data protection standards of the destination country or international organization; (3) where it is necessary for the performance of a contract to which the data subject is a party, or in order to take steps at the request of the data subject prior to entering into a contract; (4) where it is for compliance with a contract between the data controller and other Persons or juristic persons for the interests of the data subject; (5) where it is to prevent or suppress a danger to the life, body, or health of the data subject or other Persons, when the data subject is incapable of giving the consent at such time; (6) where it is necessary for carrying out the activities in relation to substantial public interest. In the event that there is a problem with regard to the adequacy of personal data protection standards of the destination country or international organization, such problem shall be submitted to the Committee to decide. The decision made by the Committee may be reviewed when there is a new evidence convincing that the destination country or international organization. that receives such Personal Data has developed adequate Personal Data protection standards. According to section 16(5) of the Act, the Personal Data Protection Committee (PDPC) has the power to announce and establish criteria for providing protection of Personal Data that is sent or transferred to a foreign country, including the list of adequate jurisdictions.

impact: Thailand's Personal Data Protection Committee (PDPC) published a subordinate regulation regarding cross-border transfer of personal data under the Personal Data Protection Act. The Notification prescribes the criteria to designate whitelisted jurisdiction or international organization having adequate level of protection. Specifically, Clause 4 of the Notification provides that in the event that the data controller sends or transfers personal data to a foreign country, the destination country or international organization that receives such personal data shall have adequate data protection standards in accordance with the criteria for the protection of personal data as prescribed in this notification, except in the following circumstances: (1) when it is for compliance with the law; (2) where the consent of the data subject has been obtained, provided that the data subject has been informed of the inadequate personal data protection standards of the destination country or international organization; (3) where it is necessary for the performance of a contract to which the data subject is a party, or in order to take steps at the request of the data subject prior to entering into a contract; (4) where it is for compliance with a contract between the data controller and other persons or juristic persons for the interests of the data subject; (5) where it is to prevent or suppress a danger to the life, body, or health of the data subject or other persons, when the data subject is incapable of giving the consent at such time; or (6) where it is necessary for carrying out the activities in relation to substantial public interest. Moreover, Clause 5 outlines two criteria for assessing whether a foreign country has adequate data protection standards: (1) Its data protection laws must be at least no less stringent as Thailand's, ensuring robust obligations for Data Controllers and effective enforcement of Data Subject rights, including legal remedies. (2) It must have a dedicated authority to enforce these data protection laws and regulations.

impact: Thailand's Personal Data Protection Committee (PDPC) published a subordinate regulation regarding cross-border transfer of personal data under the Personal Data Protection Act. The Notification concerns about the binding corporate rules (BCRs) and appropriate safeguards to transfer data in exemption of Section 28 of the PDPA. Part 1 of the Notification focuses on BCR. Personal data can be transferred to affiliated business or group undertaking if they have issued BCR which have been reviewed and certified by the PDPC (Clause 5) The BCR must be submitted for review and approval, and must meet the following criteria (Clause 7): (1) A legally binding privacy policy for all parties involved (e.g., processors, senders, receivers, employees) that complies with data protection laws. (2) A guarantee for data protection, data subject rights, and a proper complaint mechanism for cross-border transfers. (3) Security measures that meet the minimum standards set by Thailand’s data protection laws. Part 2 focuses on Approprite Safeguards provides that the sender or transferer must implement Appropriate Safeguards to protect data subjects' rights and ensure effective legal remedies (Clause 8). These safeguards must be legally binding and can take several forms: (1) Standard Contractual Clauses (SCC): Contracts must include key provisions such as compliance with data protection laws, robust security measures, and specific obligations for data processors and controllers (e.g., following instructions, notifying breaches, and handling data upon contract termination). They must also guarantee effective legal remedies for data subjects, aligning with recognized models like the ASEAN or EU GDPR clauses. (2) Certification: This involves meeting PDPC-established standards for cross-border transfers, ensuring the safeguards are legally enforceable. (3) Code of Conduct: Used for transfers between government agencies, this must also provide binding and enforceable data protection measures. In essence, Part 2 ensures that all methods of safeguarding data in cross-border transfers are legally robust, protect personal data, uphold data subject rights, and allow for effective complaint and remediation mechanisms.

impact: The Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) of Thailand was published in the Government Gazette on 27 May 2019 and fully entry into force on 1 June 2022. Thai PDPA, a general rule on data protection, was drafted based on EU Regulation 2016/679 (GDPR) and governs how personal data is processed, collected, used, disclosed, and transferred. For example, Section 19 states that the Data Controller shall not collect, use, or disclose personal data unless the data subject has given explicit consent, which can be in the written statement or via electronic means. The PDPA will join a suite with other legislations related to the digital economy: cybersecurity, consumer protection, etc. Those who violate or fail to comply with the PDPA will incur penalties, including civil, criminal, and administrative liabilities (Chapter VII Penalties). However, the PDPA shall not apply to operations of data undertaken by a credit bureau company (Section 4.6). Therefore, the details of a particular issue are in the Credit Information Business Operation Act. Moreover, before PDPA, data protection is regulated under specific laws, including the National Health Act (personal health information), Credit Information Business Operation Act (credit information), Telecommunications Business Act (personal information under the telecom sector), Commission of Computer-Related Offences Act (computer data, computer traffic data), and the Cyber Security Maintenance Act (computer data, computer system).

If there is a person who breaches the right of a service user, the licensee or the Commission shall take action to terminate such breach and inform the user promptly. impact: The Cyber Security Maintenance Act is to efficiently protect cybersecurity and to establish approaches to protect and mitigate the risk of Cyber Threats which affect the national security and public order. The Act establishes the "National Cyber Security Committee" (NCSC) and the Coordinating with national and international agencies (CRC) (Section 5 and Section 12). The NCSC is primarily responsible for proposing and overseeing cybersecurity policies, setting standards, enhancing expertise, and coordinating efforts both nationally and internationally (Section 9). The CRC focuses more on monitoring and managing specific cybersecurity threats, particularly at a critical level. It regulates national cybersecurity agencies, sets operational standards, defines the duties of organizations, and analyzes cyber threats to recommend actions to the Committee (Section 13). Additionally, the Act also establishes an Office of the National Cybersecurity Committee as a Government Agency who is a juristic person and not a government sector entity or a state enterprise to responsible for administrative, academic, meeting, and secretarial tasks of the Committee and the CRC (Sections 20 and 22). Moreover, several aspects of cybersecurity have been addressed under the Act's Chapter 3 (Maintaining cybersecurity), consisting of policies and plans (Part 1), management (Part 2), critical information infrastructure (Part 3) and coping with cyber threats (Part 4). Those who commit offences under this Act shall be usjbect to fine and/or imprisonment as prescribed under Chapter 4 (Penalty provisions).

impact: Under Chapter X Penalties, Section 74 Any person who commits an act of illegal interception, utilization or disclosure of message, information or any other data by means of telecommunications shall be liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years or to a fine not exceeding four hundred thousand Baht or to both. Section 77 The Commission shall have the power to settle all offences under this Act for which the penalty is the imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months. In this regard, the Commission may appoint a sub-committee to settle the offence on its behalf, and may prescribe the settlement criteria or any condition for the performance of duties of the sub- committee.

laws: Notification of the National Cybersecurity Committee Regarding Standards and Guidelines for Promoting the Development of Cybersecurity Service Systems B.E. 2566 (ประกาศคณะกรรมการการรักษาความมั่นคงปลอดภัยไซเบอร์แห่งชาติ (กมช.) เรื่องมาตรฐานและแนวทางส่งเสริมพัฒนาระบบการให้บริการเกี่ยวกับการรักษาความมั่นคงปลอดภัยไซเบอร์ พ.ศ. 2566)
impact: This Notification is issued under the Cybersecurity Act to provide certification for the cybersecurity service providers. Cybersecurity service providers who are certified for quality in cybersecurity must meet the criteria outlined in this notification. Quality certification is not a form of authorization (Clause 4). There are three levels of certification: (i) initial certification, (ii) advanced certification, and (iii) high-level certification. The i and ii certification can be provided to a natural person or a juristic person, while the (iii) shall be provided only to a juristic person (Clause 5). The applicant shall submitted the required documents, such as work experience certificate and documents demonstrating expertise as prescribed under Clause 6. Once the certification is issued, each type has expiray date and can be renewed (Clause 11 and Clause 13).

laws: Notification of the National Cyber Security Committee Regarding tandards for Defining the Security Category for Data or Information Systems B.E.2566 (ประกาศคณะกรรมการการรักษาความมั่นคงปลอดภัยไซเบอร์แห่งชาติ (กมช.)เรื่องมาตรฐานการกำหนดคุณลักษณะความมั่นคงปลอดภัยไซเบอร์ให้แก่ข้อมูลหรือระบบสารสนเทศ พ.ศ. 2566)

Notification of the National Cyber Security Committee Regarding Minimum Standards for Data and Information Systems B.E.2566 (ประกาศคณะกรรมการการรักษาความมั่นคงปลอดภัยไซเบอร์แห่งชาติ (กมช.) เรื่อง มาตรฐานขั้นต่ำของข้อมูลหรือระบบสารสนเทศ พ.ศ. 2566)
impact: The Notification of the National Cyber Security Committee Regarding Minimum Standards for Data and Information Systems B.E.2566 is issued under the Cybersecurity Act. This Notification prescribes a risk-based classification system for organizations' data or information systems, assessing three key security objectives: (i) confidentiality, (ii) integrity, and (iii) availability (Clause 4). Specifically, organization refers to state agency, public or private supervising organizations, and critical information infrastructure organizations. Each objective is evaluated across three risk levels (low, medium, and high) based on the potential impact on financial value, reputation, user base, operational capacity, and public order (Clauses 5 and 6). Organizations must assess all types of data handled and set the security category based on the highest risk level. The security category should be reviewed at least every three years, with results documented (Clauses 7 and 8). The Notification of the National Cyber Security Committee Regarding Minimum Standards for Data and Information Systems B.E.2566 is also issued under the Cybersecurity Act. After the Committee has identified the risk-based classification system of information system, the Comittee shall publish the minimum standards for data and information system (Clause 4). These measures involve, for example, conducting risk assessments, developing incident response plans, implementing access control and system hardining, and strengthening systems for low impact levels. For medium and high impact levels, additional steps are required such as cybersecurity audits, remote connection and removable storage for medium level, while vulnerability assessment and penetration testing, third party management, information sharing, and resilience and recovery are required for high level (Clause 4).

laws: Notification of the National Cyber Security Committee Regarding Characteristics, Duties, and Responsibilities of the Computer Emergency Response Team for Organizations of Critical Information Infrastructure and Related Missions and Services B.E.2564 (ประกาศคณะกรรมการการรักษาความมั่นคงปลอดภัยไซเบอร์แห่งชาติ (กมช.) เรื่องลักษณะหน้าที่และความรับผิดชอบของศูนย์ประสานการรักษาความมั่นคงปลอดภัยระบบคอมพิวเตอร์สำหรับหน่วยงานโครงสร้างพื้นฐานสำคัญทางสารสนเทศและภารกิจหรือให้บริการที่เกี่ยวข้อง พ.ศ.2564)
impact: This Notification is issued under the Cybersecurity Act to prescribe the roles and responsibilities of the Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT) for Organizations of Critical Information Infrastructure (CII) in Thailand. This regulation applies to government agencies, regulators, and public/ private organizations involved in critical information infrastructure (CII) in Thailand. It stipulates that relevant government agencies or regulators of Organizations of Critical Information Infrastructure in each sector must establish CERTs for CIIs, ensuring they meet prescribed characteristics, duties, and responsibilities (Clause 3). The CERTs shall coordinate with Thailand Computer Emergency Response (Attached enclosure, Clause 5).

laws: Notification of the National Cyber Security Committee Regarding Establishment, Duties, and Powers of the Thailand Computer Emergency Response Team (ThaiCERT) B.E.2564 (ประกาศคณะกรรมการการรักษาความมั่นคงปลอดภัยไซเบอร์แห่งชาติ (กมช.) เรื่อง การจัดตั้งหน้าที่และอำนาจของศูนย์ประสานการรักษาความมั่นคงปลอดภัยระบบคอมพิวเตอร์แห่งชาติ พ.ศ. 2564)
impact: This Notification is issued under the Cybersecurity Act to establish the Thailand Computer Emergency Response Team (ThaiCERT) as a unit of the National Cyber Security Agency to monitor cybersecurity risks, to track, analyze and process information related to cyber incidents, and to issue incident warnings. ThaiCERT duties and powers are available under Clause 5, including implement measures to prevent cybersecurity risks, and acting as a center of incident reporting when cyber incident occurs (For more information, see Clause 5).

laws: Notification of the National Cyber Security Committee Regarding Characteristics and Measures for Prevention, Response, Assessment, Eradication, and Containment of Cyber Incidents at Each Level B.E. 2564 (ประกาศคณะกรรมการการรักษาความมั่นคงปลอดภัยไซเบอร์แห่งชาติ (กมช.) เรื่อง ลักษณะภัยคุกคามทางไซเบอร์ มาตรการป้องกัน รับมือ ประเมิน ปราบปราม และระงับภัยคุกคามทางไซเบอร์แต่ละระดับ พ.ศ. 2564)
impact: This Notification is issued under the Cybersecurity Act to identify the details of cyber incident characteristics (non-critical level, the critical level, and the crisis level) and measures for prevention, response, assessment, eradication, and containment of cyber incidents at each level (Clause 3). Under Enclosure 1 Regarding Characteristics and Assessment of Cyber Incidents at Each Level, the level of a cyber incident relies on four factors: impact on devices or operational systems, impacts on system data, system recovery ability, and impacts on customers or users. Characteristics and guideline for impact assessment are implemented. Under Enclosure 2 Regarding Measures for Prevention, Response, Assessment, Eradication and Containment of Cyber Indicents at Each level, incident handling involves 4 key steps: prepare and protect, detect and analyze, contain/ eradicate, and recovery, and post-indicent activity. Additionally, timeframes for incident notification and report are specified. For instance, initial notification for all incidents via established channel (within the timeframe) shall be 30 minutes and the report submission to the Regulator and the National Cybersecurity Agency shall be within 2 or 4 hours, respectively.

laws: Notification of the National Telecommunications Commission regarding Telecommunications Service Users' Rights Concerning Personal Information Rights to Privacy and Freedom of Communication B.E.2566 (ประกาศกสทช. เรื่องมาตรการคุ้มครองสิทธิของผู้ใช้บริการโทรคมนาคมเกี่ยวกับข้อมูลส่วนบุคคลสิทธิในความเป็นส่วนตัวและเสรีภาพในการสื่อสารถึงกันโดยทางโทรคมนาคม พ.ศ. 2566)
impact: The Notification regarding Telecommunications Service Users' Rights Concerning Personal Information Rights to Privacy and Freedom of Communication B.E.2566 (2023) repealed the Notification regarding Telecommunications Service Users' Rights Concerning Personal Information Rights to Privacy and Freedom of Communication B.E.2549 (2006) (Clause 2). Regarding the data retention requirement, Clause 11 provides that a licensee must retain users' personal data related to their service usage for at least 90 days throughout the period of service usage. However, if a user files a complaint regarding telecommunications service usage, requiring personal data to verify the accuracy of service usage, billing, or service quality assessment, the licensee must retain the data only as necessary for resolving the complaint. This retention period must not exceed two years from the date the complaint is filed. In cases where telecommunications services are terminated, the licensee must retain the users' personal data for at least 90 days from the contract termination date. However, if necessary, or if there are outstanding payments, the licensee must retain the data but not beyond two years from the contract termination date, unless another law requires a different retention period.

laws: Computer-Related Crime Act B.E.2550 (พระราชบัญญัติ ว่าด้วยการกระทำความผิดเกี่ยวกับคอมพิวเตอร์ พ.ศ.2550)
other_urls: https://www.mdes.go.th/law/detail/3516-พระราชบัญญัติว่าด้วยการกระทำความผิดเกี่ยวกับคอมพิวเตอร์-พ-ศ--๒๕๕๐
impact: Section 26 of the Commission of Computer-Related Offences Act 2007 (so-called Computer Crimes Act 2007) defines 'Computer Traffic Data' as data in relation to the communication of computer system or the origin, time, duration, type of service, or else related to the computer system. The Act requires a service provider to retain computer traffic data for not less than 90 days from the date when the data was entered into the computer system. If necessary, the competent official may order any service provider to retain computer traffic data for a period exceeding 90 days but not exceeding 2 years as a matter of an individually exceptional case and on an ad hoc basis. The service provider shall maintain client data which is necessary for identifying the client since his or her first use of service and shall maintain such data for not less than 90 days as from the ending date of service. Those who fail to comply with this measure shall be liable to a fine not exceeding 500,000 Thai Baht (around 16,599 USD). (**Remark: The Ministry of Information and Communications Technology (ICT) currently is the Ministry of Digital Economy and Society (MDES).)

laws: Notification of the Ministry of Information and Communications Technology Regarding Computer Traffic Data Retention Criterias of Service Providers B.E.2564
other_urls: https://www.mdes.go.th/law/detail/4727-ประกาศกระทรวงดิจิทัลเพื่อเศรษฐกิจและสังคม-เรื่อง-หลักเกณฑ์การเก็บรักษาข้อมูลจราจรทางคอมพิวเตอร์ของผู้ให้บริการ-พ-ศ--๒๕๖๔
impact: The Notification of the Ministry of Information and Communications Technology B.E.2564 repealed the existing Notification B.E.2550 (Clause 3). Clause 5 provides that Certain service providers must retain computer traffic data in accordance with the specifications in Annex B, including telecom and broadcast carriers, access service providers, host service providers, internet cafe providers, online application store providers, social media service providers, content and application service providers, cloud computing service providers and digital service providers (Clause 6 and Clause 7). In general cases, service providers must retain computer traffic data for at least 90 days from the date it enters the system (Clause 12.1). If there is reason to suspect a violation of this Act or crimes related to national security, terrorism, transnational crime, or public order, officials may order service providers to retain specific user traffic data for up to six months per extension, but not exceeding two years in total (Clause 12.2). The service providers must securely store traffic data with integrity and access control, prevent unauthorized modifications, appoint a liaison for legal compliance, and ensure user identification, even for proxy or Wi-Fi services. Specifically, the service provider shall ensure that traffic data retention enables the identification and authentication of individual users. This includes logging services such as Proxy Servers, Network Address Translation (NAT), Proxy Cache, Cache Engine, or Free services (Clause 9). Note: Annex A lists down types and examples of service providers, such as VOIP, mobile service providers, Internet data center, Game online, App store, Google play, Chatbot, Telegram, Facebook, Youtube, Linkedin, Instagram, Line, MSN Messenger, Whatsapp, Web board, Blog, Internet Banking, and E-commerce service providers. Service providers must retain traffic data from the effective date of this notification. However, Internet cafés must comply within 1 year, and digital service providers within 180 days of its entry into force (Clause 13).

impact: The Credit Information Business Operation Act 2002 stipulates the requirements for controlling and processing credit information. Section 13 states that the credit information company, information controller, or processor are not allowed to process the information that is older than that prescribed in the Notification of the Credit Information Protection Committee. Similarly, the processing period shall not exceed 3 years after receiving the credit information (Clause 3 of the Notification in 2014). In addition, section 17(6) of the Credit Information Act requires that a credit information company or a person assigned to process information shall set up at least a system of recording and reporting the result of every access to the credit information. The information recording must keep for at least 2 years from the date of access to the information.

laws: Personal Data Protection Act B.E.2562 (พระราชบัญญัติคุ้มครองข้อมูลส่วนบุคคล พ.ศ. 2562)

impact: The appointment of a Data Protection Officer (DPO) is a mandatory condition under the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA). Section 41 of the Act specifies that the data controller and data processor shall designate a data protection officer in the following circumstances: the activities such as collection, use, or disclosure of the personal data. The duty of the DPO, including: advise the data controller and data processor, investigate the performance of the data controller and data processor, coordinate and cooperate with the Office or the Personal Data Protection Committee (PDPC) when there are problems and keep confidentiality of the personal data (Section 42).

laws: Cyber Security Maintenance Act B.E.2562 (พระราชบัญญัติ การรักษาความมั่นคงปลอดภัยไซเบอร์ พ.ศ.2562)
other_urls: https://www.ncsa.or.th/กฏหมาย-ข้อบังคับ-และประก.html
impact: Section 64 of the Cyber Security Maintenance Act (CSA) B.E.2562 states that, if it is necessary for the prevention, handling, and reduction of cyber threat risks, the Cyber Security Supervisory Committee (CSSC) shall order State agencies to provide information in their possession and related to cybersecurity maintenance. Also, in Section 66, the CSSC has the power to carry out or order competent officials to carry out operations, only to the extent necessary for preventing cyber threats, in the following matters: (1) to enter a place for inspection upon written notification; (2) to gain access to computer data, computer systems, or other related data, make copies, or screening; (3) to test the functionality of computers or computer systems; (4) to seize or attach, only to the extent necessary, computers, computer systems, or equipment, not exceeding 30 days. To carry out activities under (2), (3), (4) must file a motion to the competent court. However, in case of emergency and the threat is critical to cybersecurity, the Secretary-General shall take immediate action to the extent necessary for preventing and remedying damage in advance without filing a motion with the Court (Section 68).

laws: Computer-Related Crime Act B.E.2550 (พระราชบัญญัติ ว่าด้วยการกระทำความผิดเกี่ยวกับคอมพิวเตอร์ พ.ศ.2550)

impact: Section 18 of the Commission of Computer-Related Offences Act (so-called Computer Crimes Acts) provides that, when there is reasonable ground to believe that there is a violation of the Act, competent officials have the power to do: (1) to address written inquiry or issue a summons on a person connected with the offender; (2) to summon computer traffic data from providers of services; (3) to order a service provider to hand over to the competent official data concerning users; (4) to make a copy of computer data, or computer traffic data from the computer system (5) to hand over such computer data from a person having in possession or custody (6) to inspect and access a computer system, computer data, computer traffic data, or equipment used for retaining computer data (7) to decryption computer data (8) to seize or attach a computer system as necessary for identifying details of the offense The person receiving a request from the competent official shall take action in response to the request without delay. Moreover, section 19 of the Act provides that the officials have the authority to access the computer data, computer traffic data from a computer system without filing a court petition. Only the power according to Section 18(4), (5), (6), (7), and (8) requires to apply motion to the court. The Act applies to Computer data, computer traffic data/ Telecommunication and Broadcast carrier, Access Service Provider, Host Service Provider, Content Service provider, and Application Service Providers. (*Remark: Sections 18 and 19 of the Commission of Computer-Related Offences Act 2007 is repealed and replaced by the information in Section 13 of Thailand's Computer-Related Crimes Act (No.2) 2017.)

laws: National Intelligence Act B.E.2562 (พระราชบัญญัติข่าวกรองแห่งชาติ พ.ศ.2562)
impact: The National Intelligence Act B.E.2562 gives the power to the National Intelligence Agency to perform duties related to activities on intelligence operations, civil security safeguard and monitoring the situations which affect the national security (Section 5). The National Intelligence Agency may request public agencies or any person to submit information or documents relevant to national security within a specified period (Section 6). In cases where it is necessary to obtain such information, the Agency is authorized to undertake any necessary actions by adopting electronic, scientific, telecommunication devices, or other technology tools to obtain such information. Regulations, means and requirements of the proceeding shall be in accordance with rules set by the Director with the approval of the Prime Minister. The proceedings under this section, if performing duties or acting in good faith, reasonably and for the benefit of the national security or the public safety, are considered legitimate.
